synthesis.de: In Sachen KI verlasse ich mich auf mein eigenes Urteil und meine eigenen Prüfungen statt auf Fachleute und offizielle Stellen.

clarification.en: This statement is about where you place the final word on AI matters: in your own judgement or in expert opinion. It does not ask whether you listen to experts, but whose view you ultimately rely on when forming your position.
clarification.fr: Cette affirmation porte sur ce qui a le dernier mot pour vous en matière d'IA : votre propre jugement ou l'avis des experts. Elle ne demande pas si vous écoutez les experts, mais sur quel avis vous vous appuyez finalement pour vous forger une position.
clarification.de: Diese Aussage betrifft die Frage, was für Sie bei KI-Themen das letzte Wort hat: Ihr eigenes Urteil oder die Meinung von Fachleuten. Sie fragt nicht, ob Sie Fachleuten zuhören, sondern auf wessen Sicht Sie sich letztlich stützen, wenn Sie sich eine Position bilden.

clarification.fr: Cette affirmation porte sur les motivations des organismes de surveillance : les organisations chargées de veiller sur l'IA. Elle demande si vous croyez qu'ils font passer leurs propres intérêts avant ceux du public. Il s'agit de leurs motivations, pas de leur compétence.

figures.name: Léon Tolstoï
figures.presentation: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910), Russian novelist turned moral-religious critic, excommunicated by the Orthodox Church in 1901, addressed peasants and educated classes alike from his estate. His wave was the railway and the telegraph binding Imperial Russia — a society nine-tenths peasant — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was skeptical on two joined grounds: class — the telegraph served the “so-called cultured class” while the peasant heard “only the buzzing of the wires” — and moral-religious, judging technology by conscience and the Gospel; his instrument was voluntary moral renunciation, not law or force. No caricature: at 67 he learned to ride a bicycle with childlike pleasure. What instructs is the discipline of his recurring test — who benefits, who bears the cost, and by what standard a society should judge what it is told to call progress.
figures.epoch: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910) was a Russian novelist and moral-religious thinker whose later work turned from fiction toward social and ethical criticism. Alongside the fiction for which he was internationally known, he produced a substantial body of essays and treatises — "Progress and the Definition of Education" (1862), the autobiographical "A Confession" (written 1879–1882), the treatise "What Shall We Do?" (1886), "The Kingdom of God Is Within You" (1894), and "The Slavery of Our Times" (1900) — that made him a leading voice of Christian anarchism and pacifism. Writing from his estate in Imperial Russia, he addressed peasants and educated classes alike, and his moral authority extended well beyond literature. In 1901 the Russian Orthodox Church excommunicated him, a measure of how far his religious dissent unsettled the established institutions of his time.

figures.name: John Perry Barlow
figures.presentation: John Perry Barlow (1947–2018), Grateful Dead lyricist, Wyoming rancher and co-founder of the Electronic Frontier Foundation (1990), became a recognised voice of early cyberspace through The Economy of Ideas (1994) and A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace (1996). His wave was the internet’s leap from research networks to mass medium, met through The WELL and the legal frictions of a networking public — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. The record shows an unqualified enthusiast: cyberspace an emancipatory civilisation of the mind, beyond state sovereignty, ordered by ethics rather than imposed law — matched by years of unpaid civil-liberties advocacy. What instructs is this documented experiment in maximal techno-optimism: a utopian partly right about freedom, partly wrong about sovereignty, faithful to his thesis to the end.
figures.epoch: John Perry Barlow (1947-2018) was an American lyricist for the Grateful Dead, a Wyoming cattle rancher, and an internet-civil-liberties advocate whose life spanned strikingly different worlds. An early member of the pioneering online community The WELL, he co-founded the Electronic Frontier Foundation in 1990 with Mitch Kapor and John Gilmore, an organisation dedicated to defending civil liberties on networked systems, and he served on its board until his death; in 2012 he also co-founded the Freedom of the Press Foundation. His standing in the emerging digital culture rested less on technical work than on words: two texts made him a recognised voice of early cyberspace thought, A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace (Davos, 1996) and the essay The Economy of Ideas (Wired, 1994). He occupied an unusual position between counterculture, ranching and the networked frontier, which lent his advocacy its distinctive rhetorical register.

figures.name: Alan Turing
figures.presentation: Alan Turing (1912–1954), English mathematician, stood where mathematics, the first stored-program computers and the public debate over thinking machines met — a limit case in this study, since his wave is the direct ancestor of today's AI. His stance was confident advocacy with a method: replace the ill-defined “can machines think?” with a measurable test, predict openly, and demand “fair play for the machine.” He named the danger plainly — machines might “take control” — yet remained an advocate rather than a brake. What instructs is the lucidity: forecast, criterion and acknowledged risk held together in one stance.
figures.epoch: Alan Mathison Turing (1912–1954) was an English mathematician who worked at the centre of Britain's postwar computing effort. His documented career unfolded inside the state scientific establishment: wartime service at Bletchley Park, the National Physical Laboratory, and the University of Manchester. He addressed the London Mathematical Society on the prospects of automatic computing machines in February 1947, published "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" in the philosophy journal Mind in 1950, and wrote the first programming manual for the Manchester Electronic Computer (Mark II) in 1951. He also circulated the National Physical Laboratory report "Intelligent Machinery" (1948) and took part in BBC radio discussions of machine thinking in 1951 and 1952. He thus stood at the meeting point of mathematics, the emerging discipline of computing, and the public debate over whether machines could think.

title.en: Do not trust in-house AI safety promises: make independent audits the law
title.fr: Ne pas croire les promesses internes de sûreté de l'IA : imposer des audits indépendants par la loi

text.en: In January 2026 testimony on New York's AI Act, Chowdhury argues that AI governance belongs in 'enforceable obligations, not voluntary ethics pledges.' The most meaningful safety improvements, she testifies, come when evaluations are run by bodies structurally independent of product and revenue teams — so companies' and their experts' in-house safety assurances should not be taken on trust but checked by mandatory independent audit. She personifies 'trust, but independently verify.'
text.fr: Dans son témoignage de janvier 2026 sur la loi new-yorkaise sur l'IA, Rumman Chowdhury soutient que la gouvernance de l'IA relève d'« obligations contraignantes, et non de promesses éthiques volontaires ». Les améliorations les plus significatives, témoigne-t-elle, viennent d'évaluations menées par des entités structurellement indépendantes des équipes produit et commerciales — les garanties internes des entreprises et de leurs experts ne doivent donc pas être crues sur parole, mais vérifiées par des audits indépendants obligatoires. Elle incarne le « faire confiance, mais vérifier de façon indépendante ».

arguments.reference: Testimony of Dr. Rumman Chowdhury before the New York State Senate Standing Committee on Internet and Technology, on the New York Artificial Intelligence Act, 15 January 2026.
arguments.quote: The most meaningful improvements have come when evaluations are run by entities structurally independent of product and revenue teams and when results are tied to concrete risk-mitigation obligations.

title.en: Dutch tax algorithm wrongly branded 26,000 parents as fraudsters; government resigned
title.fr: Un algorithme du fisc néerlandais a accusé à tort 26 000 parents de fraude ; le gouvernement a démissionné

text.en: The Dutch tax administration used automated risk profiling, including a risk-scoring algorithm, to flag suspected childcare-benefit fraud; roughly 26,000 parents were wrongly treated as fraudsters, with discriminatory effects linked to nationality and dual citizenship. The parliamentary inquiry report 'Ongekend onrecht' ('Unprecedented Injustice', 17 December 2020) found fundamental institutional failures, and the entire Rutte III government resigned on 15 January 2021. The case is widely cited to show that public institutions themselves can deploy and defend harmful algorithmic systems for years.
text.fr: L'administration fiscale néerlandaise a utilisé un profilage automatisé des risques, dont un algorithme de scoring, pour repérer des fraudes présumées aux allocations de garde d'enfants ; environ 26 000 parents ont été traités à tort comme fraudeurs, avec des effets discriminatoires liés à la nationalité et à la double nationalité. Le rapport d'enquête parlementaire « Ongekend onrecht » (« Une injustice sans précédent », 17 décembre 2020) a constaté des défaillances institutionnelles fondamentales, et l'ensemble du gouvernement Rutte III a démissionné le 15 janvier 2021. Ce cas est largement cité pour montrer que les institutions publiques elles-mêmes peuvent déployer et défendre pendant des années des systèmes algorithmiques préjudiciables.

arguments.reference: Parliamentary Inquiry Committee on Childcare Allowance, report 'Unprecedented Injustice', House of Representatives of the Netherlands, 17 December 2020 (official English translation)

title.en: Extinction fears are a lobbying tool against open-source competition
title.fr: La peur de l'extinction, outil de lobbying contre la concurrence open source

arguments.person: Andrew Ng, co-founder of Google Brain, professor at Stanford University

text.en: In October 2023, Andrew Ng — co-founder of Google Brain and professor at Stanford — argued in an interview with the Australian Financial Review that some large technology companies amplify fears of AI-driven human extinction in order to obtain regulation that would weaken open-source competition. His warning is a contemporary version of the regulatory-capture argument: rules presented as protecting the public may in fact be shaped to serve incumbent interests.
text.fr: En octobre 2023, Andrew Ng — cofondateur de Google Brain et professeur à Stanford — a soutenu dans une interview à l'Australian Financial Review que certaines grandes entreprises technologiques amplifient les peurs d'une extinction de l'humanité par l'IA afin d'obtenir une réglementation qui affaiblirait la concurrence open source. Son avertissement est une version contemporaine de l'argument de la capture réglementaire : des règles présentées comme protégeant le public peuvent en réalité être façonnées pour servir les intérêts des acteurs établis.

arguments.reference: Interview with The Australian Financial Review, October 2023; quoted verbatim by SiliconANGLE, 31 October 2023
arguments.quote: There are definitely large tech companies that would rather not have to try to compete with open source [AI], so they're creating fear of AI leading to human extinction.

justification.en: The press made personal reading a majority act of judgement against authority: sola scriptura, the Bible in the vernacular (Luther's New Testament, 1522), a flood of Flugschriften (several hundred thousand copies of Luther's writings alone between 1517 and 1520). Free cities, princes and peasants read, compared and decided for themselves; the institutional reaction (the Index, 1559) came after most German and Scandinavian lands had already chosen by their own examination.
justification.fr: La presse fait de la lecture personnelle un acte majoritaire de jugement contre l'autorité : sola scriptura, Bible en langue vulgaire (Nouveau Testament de Luther, 1522), déluge de Flugschriften (plusieurs centaines de milliers d'exemplaires des seuls écrits de Luther entre 1517 et 1520). Villes libres, princes et paysans lisent, comparent et tranchent eux-mêmes ; la réaction institutionnelle (Index, 1559) arrive après que la majorité des espaces germaniques et scandinaves a déjà choisi selon son propre examen.

justification.en: The network made checking for oneself a mass norm — forums, comparison sites, 'Doctor Google', an encyclopedia written by its readers (Wikipedia, 2001), blogs against the established press. Most internet users trusted their own searches more than official bodies, a trend the next period would call the crisis of intermediaries.
justification.fr: Le réseau installe la vérification par soi-même comme norme de masse — forums, comparateurs, « Docteur Google », encyclopédie écrite par ses lecteurs (Wikipédia, 2001), blogs contre presse installée. La majorité des internautes fait plus confiance à ses propres recherches qu'aux organismes officiels, tendance que la période suivante nommera crise des intermédiaires.

examples.fr: Par exemple, si une agence publique annonce qu'elle surveille l'IA utilisée dans les hôpitaux ou les écoles, cela vous donne-t-il le sentiment que les choses sont bien gérées, ou non ?
examples.de: Wenn zum Beispiel eine öffentliche Behörde ankündigt, dass sie die in Krankenhäusern oder Schulen eingesetzte KI überwacht: Gibt Ihnen das die Zuversicht, dass die Dinge richtig gehandhabt werden, oder nicht?

text.en: When recognised experts state that an AI system is safe, I generally trust their judgement.
text.fr: Quand des experts reconnus déclarent qu'un système d'IA est sûr, je fais généralement confiance à leur jugement.
text.de: Wenn anerkannte Fachleute erklären, dass ein KI-System sicher ist, vertraue ich in der Regel ihrem Urteil.

clarification.en: This statement is about recognised experts, such as scientists or specialised engineers, saying an AI system is safe. It asks whether you generally accept their judgement in that situation. 'Generally' matters: it is about your usual attitude, not rare exceptions.
clarification.fr: Cette affirmation porte sur des experts reconnus, comme des scientifiques ou des ingénieurs spécialisés, déclarant qu'un système d'IA est sûr. Elle demande si, dans cette situation, vous acceptez généralement leur jugement. « Généralement » compte : il s'agit de votre attitude habituelle, pas des rares exceptions.
clarification.de: Diese Aussage betrifft anerkannte Fachleute, etwa aus der Wissenschaft oder aus spezialisierten Ingenieurberufen, die erklären, dass ein KI-System sicher ist. Sie fragt, ob Sie deren Urteil in dieser Situation in der Regel akzeptieren. „In der Regel“ ist wichtig: Es geht darum, wie Sie üblicherweise reagieren, nicht um seltene Ausnahmen.

anchor_low.de: Die Antwort 0 bedeutet, dass eine Erklärung von Fachleuten, ein KI-System sei sicher, für Sie kein Gewicht hat; Sie verlassen sich nicht auf deren Wort.

anchor_high.en: Answering 5 means that when recognised experts say an AI system is safe, you accept their judgement without reservation.
anchor_high.fr: Répondre 5 signifie que lorsque des experts reconnus déclarent qu'un système d'IA est sûr, vous acceptez leur jugement sans réserve.
anchor_high.de: Die Antwort 5 bedeutet, dass Sie, wenn anerkannte Fachleute ein KI-System für sicher erklären, deren Urteil ohne Vorbehalt akzeptieren.

examples.en: For example, specialists state that an AI feature in cars is safe: is that enough for you to feel at ease using it?
examples.fr: Par exemple, des spécialistes déclarent qu'une fonction d'IA dans les voitures est sûre : cela vous suffit-il pour l'utiliser l'esprit tranquille ?
examples.de: Zum Beispiel erklären Fachleute, dass eine KI-Funktion in Autos sicher ist: Reicht Ihnen das, um sie beruhigt zu nutzen?

examples.en: For example, health experts say an AI tool used by doctors is reliable: would you accept its involvement in your care on that basis?
examples.fr: Par exemple, des experts de santé affirment qu'un outil d'IA utilisé par les médecins est fiable : accepteriez-vous sur cette base qu'il intervienne dans vos soins ?
examples.de: Zum Beispiel erklären Fachleute aus dem Gesundheitswesen, ein ärztlich genutztes KI-Werkzeug sei zuverlässig: Würden Sie auf dieser Grundlage akzeptieren, dass es in Ihre Behandlung einbezogen wird?

text.en: Certification of an AI system by an official body reassures me about using it.
text.fr: La certification d'un système d'IA par un organisme officiel me rassure quant à son utilisation.
text.de: Die Zertifizierung eines KI-Systems durch eine offizielle Stelle beruhigt mich im Hinblick auf seine Nutzung.

clarification.en: This statement is about official certification: a label, stamp, or approval given by an official body to an AI system. It asks whether such certification actually reassures you when deciding to use the system.
clarification.fr: Cette affirmation porte sur la certification officielle : un label, un tampon ou une approbation accordés à un système d'IA par un organisme officiel. Elle demande si cette certification vous rassure réellement au moment de décider d'utiliser ce système.
clarification.de: Diese Aussage betrifft die offizielle Zertifizierung: ein Label, ein Siegel oder eine Zulassung von einer offiziellen Stelle für ein KI-System. Sie fragt, ob eine solche Zertifizierung Sie tatsächlich beruhigt, wenn Sie über die Nutzung des Systems entscheiden.

anchor_low.en: Answering 0 means official certification of an AI system does not reassure you at all; it changes nothing in how you feel about using it.
anchor_low.fr: Répondre 0 signifie que la certification officielle d'un système d'IA ne vous rassure pas du tout ; elle ne change rien à ce que vous ressentez à l'idée de l'utiliser.
anchor_low.de: Die Antwort 0 bedeutet, dass die offizielle Zertifizierung eines KI-Systems Sie überhaupt nicht beruhigt; sie ändert nichts daran, wie Sie sich bei dem Gedanken an die Nutzung fühlen.

anchor_high.en: Answering 5 means official certification fully reassures you about using an AI system.
anchor_high.fr: Répondre 5 signifie que la certification officielle vous rassure pleinement quant à l'utilisation d'un système d'IA.
anchor_high.de: Die Antwort 5 bedeutet, dass die offizielle Zertifizierung Sie im Hinblick auf die Nutzung eines KI-Systems voll und ganz beruhigt.

examples.en: For example, an AI app for managing personal finances carries an official approval mark: does that mark make you noticeably more comfortable using it?
examples.fr: Par exemple, une application d'IA pour gérer les finances personnelles porte un label officiel d'approbation : ce label vous met-il nettement plus à l'aise pour l'utiliser ?
examples.de: Zum Beispiel trägt eine KI-App zur Verwaltung der persönlichen Finanzen ein offizielles Prüfsiegel: Fühlen Sie sich mit diesem Siegel deutlich wohler bei der Nutzung?

examples.en: For example, a certified AI translation service is offered for official documents: does the certification make a real difference to your willingness to rely on it?
examples.fr: Par exemple, un service de traduction par IA certifié est proposé pour des documents officiels : la certification change-t-elle vraiment votre disposition à vous y fier ?
examples.de: Zum Beispiel wird ein zertifizierter KI-Übersetzungsdienst für offizielle Dokumente angeboten: Macht die Zertifizierung einen echten Unterschied für Ihre Bereitschaft, sich darauf zu verlassen?

figures.name: Norman Borlaug
figures.presentation: Norman Borlaug (1914–2009), American agronomist and 1970 Nobel Peace laureate, directed the wheat-breeding work in Mexico that grew into the Green Revolution. His wave was agriculture’s synthetic-chemistry transformation — chemical fertilizer he called the fuel of its forward thrust, synthetic pesticides, improved seed — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was the enthusiast’s: deploy fast, at scale, to feed the poorest, defending transgenic crops and condemning “antiscience zealotry.” Yet the optimism was conditional and moral, not naïve: the Nobel lecture calls the Green Revolution a temporary success, a breathing space, grounded in food as a moral right. What instructs is urgency to deploy joined to an explicit statement of the technology’s limits and ethical purpose.
figures.epoch: Norman Ernest Borlaug (1914–2009) was an American agronomist and plant pathologist who directed the cooperative wheat-improvement work that developed high-yielding, disease-resistant dwarf wheat varieties, first in Mexico within the Rockefeller Foundation programme that later grew into the CIMMYT research centre. Trained in the North American land-grant scientific tradition, he became one of the most publicly recognised agricultural scientists of the mid-twentieth century, awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 for the yield gains his methods brought to wheat and rice cultivation in the developing world. His standing rested not on a single theoretical work but on a body of field-based breeding practice and on widely circulated statements of its purpose — chief among them the 1970 Nobel lecture, "The Green Revolution, Peace, and Humanity," which framed the enterprise as a moral response to hunger.

figures.name: Paul Berg
figures.presentation: Paul Berg (1926–2023), American biochemist and 1980 Nobel laureate in Chemistry, built the first recombinant DNA molecules — the opening act of genetic engineering, a technology whose promise and hazards were debated before either was fully known. Facing that uncertainty he chose a rare course: in 1974 he led the call for a voluntary moratorium on the riskiest experiments, then chaired the 1975 Asilomar Conference that resumed them under graded containment rules of the community's own making — while later resisting over-restrictive legislation. His trajectory — pause, then proceed under the field's own rules — remains the textbook case of a science governing itself before being governed, wary equally of unmanaged risk and of heavy outside control.
figures.epoch: Paul Berg (1926-2023) was an American biochemist and one of the leading molecular biologists of the postwar United States. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1980 for his fundamental studies of nucleic acids, and his Nobel Lecture, "Dissections and Reconstructions of Genes and Chromosomes" (Stockholm, 8 December 1980), documents the work for which he is best known: the construction of the first recombinant DNA molecules, joining genetic material from different organisms and reshaping the working methods of molecular biology (berg1980-nobel). Beyond the bench, he occupied a position of scientific authority in his community, chairing the National Academy of Sciences committee that examined the hazards of the new techniques and convening, as its chairman, the 1975 Asilomar Conference that set the terms under which the field would proceed (berg1974-letter, berg1975-asilomar).

quote.en: If the Asilomar exercise was a success, it was because scientists took the initiative in raising the issue rather than having it raised against them.
quote.fr: Si l'exercice d'Asilomar a été un succès, c'est parce que les scientifiques ont pris l'initiative de soulever la question plutôt que de se la voir opposer.
quote.reference: Paul Berg, « Asilomar and Recombinant DNA », NobelPrize.org, 26 août 2004

figures.name: Yoshua Bengio
figures.presentation: Yoshua Bengio (born 1964), co-founder of modern deep learning, 2018 Turing Award laureate, recorded as the field’s most-cited researcher, lived the very wave this study takes as its subject: artificial intelligence itself, whose acceleration past GPT-4-class systems he judged to have outrun precaution and governance. From inside, he revised his position on public evidence — first scientific signatory of the 2023 pause letter, Senate testimony for regulation “beyond voluntary guidelines,” chair of the 2025 International AI Safety Report — while continuing to build: the deliberately non-agentic “Scientist AI” and the nonprofit LawZero (2025). A living figure still in motion, he models how precaution and retained optimism can coexist without collapsing into boosterism or doom.
figures.epoch: Yoshua Bengio (born 1964) is one of the three researchers credited with founding modern deep learning, for which he shared the 2018 A.M. Turing Award; the dossier records him among the most-cited researchers in artificial intelligence. Rather than retreating into eminence, he has remained an active frontier researcher into his sixties, reorienting his own programme toward a new, deliberately non-agentic architecture he calls "Scientist AI" and, in June 2025, founding the nonprofit LawZero (launched with USD 30 million) to pursue safety-oriented research outside commercial pressures. He thus occupies a rare dual standing: a foundational technical author of the field and, since 2023, one of its most institutionally prominent voices on governance, chairing the international expert panel behind the 2025 International AI Safety Report while continuing to build.

title.en: Official certification of high-risk AI is now the law in Europe
title.fr: La certification officielle des IA à haut risque est désormais la loi en Europe

text.en: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the AI Act) requires high-risk AI systems to undergo a conformity assessment before being placed on the EU market (Article 43). For certain categories — notably biometric systems — assessment by an independent notified body is required when harmonised standards are not (fully) applied, and compliant systems carry the CE marking familiar from European product-safety law. The regime institutionalises the idea that official certification can give users a reasoned basis for confidence they could not obtain by individual inspection.
text.fr: Le règlement (UE) 2024/1689 (législation sur l'IA) impose aux systèmes d'IA à haut risque une évaluation de la conformité avant leur mise sur le marché européen (article 43). Pour certaines catégories — notamment les systèmes biométriques — l'évaluation par un organisme notifié indépendant est requise lorsque les normes harmonisées ne sont pas (pleinement) appliquées, et les systèmes conformes portent le marquage CE bien connu du droit européen de la sécurité des produits. Ce régime institutionnalise l'idée qu'une certification officielle peut donner aux utilisateurs une base raisonnée de confiance qu'ils ne pourraient obtenir par un examen individuel.

arguments.reference: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 43 (Conformity assessment), in force since 1 August 2024

title.en: Expert certification made flying safe (one accident per 880,000 flights); a model for AI
title.fr: La certification par des experts a rendu l'avion sûr (un accident pour 880 000 vols) ; un modèle pour l'IA

text.en: Commercial aviation is the standard example of a domain where deferring to expert safety judgement has demonstrably worked. According to IATA's 2024 Safety Report (released 26 February 2025), the all-accident rate was 1.13 per million flights — one accident per 880,000 flights across 40.6 million flights — and the five-year average improved from one accident per 456,000 flights (2011–2015) to one per 810,000 (2020–2024). This record was built on expert-run certification, audits and independent accident investigation, a model often invoked for AI assurance.
text.fr: L'aviation commerciale est l'exemple type d'un domaine où la déférence au jugement des experts en sécurité a manifestement fonctionné. Selon le rapport de sécurité 2024 de l'IATA (publié le 26 février 2025), le taux global d'accidents était de 1,13 par million de vols — un accident pour 880 000 vols sur 40,6 millions de vols — et la moyenne quinquennale s'est améliorée d'un accident pour 456 000 vols (2011–2015) à un pour 810 000 (2020–2024). Ce bilan repose sur la certification par des experts, les audits et l'enquête indépendante sur les accidents, un modèle souvent invoqué pour l'assurance de l'IA.

arguments.reference: IATA 2024 Annual Safety Report, press release, 26 February 2025

title.en: Even the maker of ChatGPT asked the US Senate to regulate AI
title.fr: Même le créateur de ChatGPT a demandé au Sénat américain de réguler l'IA

text.en: On 16 May 2023, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI (the company behind ChatGPT), testified before the US Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology and the Law. In his opening statement he explicitly called for government regulation of AI. The testimony is frequently cited as evidence that even the leading developers of AI consider public institutions indispensable for managing its risks.
text.fr: Le 16 mai 2023, Sam Altman, PDG d'OpenAI (l'entreprise derrière ChatGPT), a témoigné devant la sous-commission du Sénat américain chargée de la vie privée, de la technologie et du droit. Dans sa déclaration liminaire, il a explicitement appelé à une régulation gouvernementale de l'IA. Ce témoignage est fréquemment cité comme preuve que même les principaux développeurs d'IA considèrent les institutions publiques comme indispensables pour gérer ses risques.

arguments.reference: US Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing "Oversight of A.I.: Rules for Artificial Intelligence", 16 May 2023 (Tech Policy Press transcript)
arguments.quote: However, we think that regulatory intervention by governments will be critical to mitigate the risks of increasingly powerful models.

justification.en: European societies delegated massively to medical science and the sanitary state: compulsory vaccination laws (United Kingdom 1853, German Empire 1874, France 1902), Pasteur raised to national hero, the Institut Pasteur funded by public subscription (1886–1888, over two million francs, from the Tsar to the factory worker), official certification of serums. Anti-vaccination leagues (Leicester, 1885) existed but remained the exception confirming majority trust, upheld by the courts (Jacobson v. Massachusetts, 1905).
justification.fr: Les sociétés européennes délèguent massivement à la science médicale et à l'État sanitaire : lois de vaccination obligatoire (Royaume-Uni 1853, Empire allemand 1874, France 1902), Pasteur élevé au rang de héros national, Institut Pasteur financé par souscription publique (1886–1888, plus de deux millions de francs, du tsar à l'ouvrier), certification officielle des sérums. Les ligues anti-vaccinales (Leicester, 1885) existent mais restent l'exception qui confirme la confiance majoritaire, confirmée par les tribunaux (Jacobson v. Massachusetts, 1905).

justification.en: After the Asilomar moratorium (1975), society agreed to entrust the experts themselves and official committees (NIH Recombinant DNA Advisory Committee, 1976; national ethics committees) with authorising or forbidding; recombinant insulin (1982) was adopted without reluctance because it was certified. Trust shifted towards the supervising body rather than towards the technology.
justification.fr: Après le moratoire d'Asilomar (1975), la société accepte de confier aux experts eux-mêmes et à des comités officiels (NIH Recombinant DNA Advisory Committee, 1976 ; comités d'éthique nationaux) le soin d'autoriser ou d'interdire ; l'insuline recombinante (1982) est adoptée sans réticence parce qu'elle est certifiée. La confiance se déplace vers l'organe de contrôle plutôt que vers la technologie.

synthesis.en: On balance, I expect AI to do more harm than good, and that future worries me.
synthesis.fr: Au total, je m'attends à ce que l'IA fasse plus de mal que de bien, et cet avenir m'inquiète.
synthesis.de: Alles in allem erwarte ich, dass KI mehr schadet als nützt, und diese Zukunft beunruhigt mich.

text.en: I believe AI will create more problems than it will solve.
text.fr: Je pense que l'IA créera plus de problèmes qu'elle n'en résoudra.
text.de: Ich glaube, dass KI mehr Probleme schaffen wird, als sie löst.

clarification.en: This statement asks you to weigh everything together: the problems AI creates against the problems it solves. It is about the overall balance you expect, not about whether some problems exist (almost everyone agrees some do).
clarification.fr: Cette affirmation vous demande de tout mettre en balance : les problèmes que l'IA crée face aux problèmes qu'elle résout. Il s'agit du bilan global que vous attendez, pas de savoir si certains problèmes existent (presque tout le monde en convient).
clarification.de: Diese Aussage bittet Sie, alles gegeneinander abzuwägen: die Probleme, die KI schafft, gegen die Probleme, die sie löst. Es geht um die Gesamtbilanz, die Sie erwarten – nicht darum, ob es überhaupt Probleme gibt (darin sind sich fast alle einig).

anchor_low.en: Answering 0 means you are convinced the opposite is true: in your view, AI will solve more problems than it creates.
anchor_low.fr: Répondre 0 signifie que vous êtes convaincu·e du contraire : selon vous, l'IA résoudra plus de problèmes qu'elle n'en créera.
anchor_low.de: Eine Antwort mit 0 bedeutet, dass Sie vom Gegenteil überzeugt sind: Aus Ihrer Sicht wird KI mehr Probleme lösen, als sie schafft.

anchor_high.en: Answering 5 means you are convinced that, all things considered, AI will create more problems than it will solve.
anchor_high.fr: Répondre 5 signifie que vous êtes convaincu·e que, tout bien pesé, l'IA créera plus de problèmes qu'elle n'en résoudra.
anchor_high.de: Eine Antwort mit 5 bedeutet, dass Sie überzeugt sind, dass KI alles in allem mehr Probleme schaffen wird, als sie löst.

examples.en: For example, at work: when you picture AI in workplaces, do you see mostly new difficulties (lost jobs, new errors) or mostly difficulties removed (tedious tasks done, help available)?
examples.fr: Par exemple, au travail : quand vous imaginez l'IA dans les milieux professionnels, voyez-vous surtout de nouvelles difficultés (emplois perdus, nouvelles erreurs) ou surtout des difficultés en moins (tâches pénibles prises en charge, aide disponible) ?
examples.de: Zum Beispiel bei der Arbeit: Wenn Sie sich KI in der Arbeitswelt vorstellen, sehen Sie vor allem neue Schwierigkeiten (verlorene Arbeitsplätze, neue Fehler) oder vor allem Schwierigkeiten, die wegfallen (mühsame Aufgaben werden erledigt, Hilfe ist verfügbar)?

examples.en: For example, in public life: do you expect AI to add more confusion (fake images, manipulation) than it removes, or the reverse?
examples.fr: Par exemple, dans la vie publique : pensez-vous que l'IA ajoutera plus de confusion (fausses images, manipulation) qu'elle n'en supprimera, ou l'inverse ?
examples.de: Zum Beispiel im öffentlichen Leben: Erwarten Sie, dass KI mehr Verwirrung stiftet (gefälschte Bilder, Manipulation), als sie beseitigt – oder umgekehrt?

text.en: I expect AI, on balance, to do lasting damage to society.
text.fr: Je m'attends à ce que, au total, l'IA cause des dommages durables à la société.
text.de: Ich erwarte, dass KI der Gesellschaft alles in allem dauerhaften Schaden zufügen wird.

clarification.en: This statement is about serious, lasting harm to society, weighed on balance: not temporary difficulties during a period of adjustment, and not one isolated harm among larger gains. It asks what you genuinely expect to happen, not what you fear might possibly happen.
clarification.fr: Cet énoncé porte sur des dommages graves et durables pour la société, considérés au total : ni des difficultés passagères pendant une période d'adaptation, ni un dommage isolé au milieu de gains plus larges. Il demande ce que vous vous attendez réellement à voir arriver, pas ce que vous craignez comme simple possibilité.
clarification.de: Diese Aussage betrifft schwere, dauerhafte Schäden für die Gesellschaft, in der Gesamtbilanz betrachtet: weder vorübergehende Schwierigkeiten in einer Übergangszeit noch einen einzelnen Schaden inmitten größerer Gewinne. Gefragt wird, was Sie wirklich erwarten – nicht, was Sie als bloße Möglichkeit befürchten.

anchor_low.en: Answering 0 means that, on balance, you do not expect AI to leave society with lasting damage.
anchor_low.fr: Répondre 0 signifie qu'au total, vous ne vous attendez pas à ce que l'IA laisse à la société des dommages durables.
anchor_low.de: Eine Antwort mit 0 bedeutet, dass Sie alles in allem nicht erwarten, dass KI der Gesellschaft dauerhafte Schäden hinterlässt.

anchor_high.en: Answering 5 means you fully expect AI, on balance, to cause damage to society that will last.
anchor_high.fr: Répondre 5 signifie que vous vous attendez pleinement à ce qu'au total, l'IA cause à la société des dommages qui dureront.
anchor_high.de: Eine Antwort mit 5 bedeutet, dass Sie voll und ganz erwarten, dass KI der Gesellschaft alles in allem Schäden zufügen wird, die bestehen bleiben.

examples.en: For example, in family life: do you expect AI to permanently weaken things like children's learning or people's ability to talk to each other, or do you expect such worries to fade?
examples.fr: Par exemple, dans la vie familiale : pensez-vous que l'IA affaiblira durablement des choses comme l'apprentissage des enfants ou la capacité des gens à se parler, ou pensez-vous que ces inquiétudes s'estomperont ?
examples.de: Zum Beispiel im Familienleben: Erwarten Sie, dass KI Dinge wie das Lernen der Kinder oder die Fähigkeit der Menschen, miteinander zu reden, dauerhaft schwächen wird – oder erwarten Sie, dass sich solche Sorgen legen?

examples.en: For example, in civic life: do you expect AI to durably damage trust in what we see and read, or do you expect society to adjust?

figures.name: Erwin Chargaff
figures.presentation: Erwin Chargaff (1905–2002), Austrian-born biochemist who established the base-composition rules of DNA, became in later life a humanistic critic estranged from the molecular biology his own discoveries had made possible. His wave was genetic engineering — recombinant DNA creating new forms of life from the early 1970s — this study’s mirror for today’s AI, promoted largely by its own developers. His stance was deep skepticism: a new form of life, once released, cannot be recalled; no one holds the right to counteract “irreversibly, the evolutionary wisdom of millions of years”; and scientists’ self-regulation cannot weigh a risk borne by all humanity. What instructs is the method more than the verdict — irreversibility first, and those who profit are not the only ones entitled to judge safety. Documentary richness, never a moral model.
figures.epoch: Erwin Chargaff (1905-2002), an Austrian-born biochemist who made his scientific career in the United States, established the base-composition regularities known as Chargaff's rules — that in DNA adenine equals thymine and cytosine equals guanine — findings his own work, drawing on chromatographic methods, made central to the study of nucleic acids. An eminent figure of mid-twentieth-century biochemistry and author of Essays on Nucleic Acids (Elsevier, 1963), he became in later life a humanistic critic and memoirist. His Heraclitean Fire: Sketches from a Life before Nature (The Rockefeller University Press, 1978) presents him as a scientist steeped in classical learning who grew estranged from the molecular biology his own discoveries had helped make possible. He remained within the scientific establishment while increasingly standing apart from it.

figures.name: Ōe Kenzaburō
figures.presentation: Ōe Kenzaburō (1935–2023), Japanese novelist and 1994 Nobel laureate in Literature, formed by the humanism of his teacher Kazuo Watanabe, became a public conscience on the atomic question with Hiroshima Notes (1965). His wave was atomic energy and weapons, met at the point of consequence, not invention — Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the 1954 Bikini test, then Fukushima in 2011 — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was victim-side across five decades: reading the atom “through the eyes of the victims of nuclear power,” and after Fukushima fusing weapons and civil nuclear power into a single refusal, carried into the ten-million-signature Sayonara Genpatsu campaign. What instructs is the method rather than the verdict: those who bear a technology’s consequences, not only its advocates, must be heard before it is scaled.
figures.epoch: Ōe Kenzaburō (1935–2023) was a Japanese novelist and essayist awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1994; his Nobel lecture, "Japan, the Ambiguous, and Myself," delivered 7 December 1994, deliberately set his work against Kawabata's earlier "Japan, the Beautiful, and Myself." Formed by the humanism of his teacher Kazuo Watanabe, a scholar of Rabelais, he built a body of fiction and reportage centred on human vulnerability and moral witness. His documentary work Hiroshima Notes, serialized in the journal Sekai in 1964–65, published by Iwanami Shoten in 1965 and read for this study in its English translation, established him as a public conscience on the atomic question. The birth of his son Hikari, who lived with a disability and found healing through music, recurs across his writing as a source of what he called "the exquisite healing power of art." He remained an engaged public intellectual until his death in 2023.

figures.name: Alfred Russel Wallace
figures.presentation: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), British naturalist and co-discoverer of evolution by natural selection, largely self-taught, was also a social reformer and, by the 1890s, a prominent public figure of British science. His wave was the germ theory and the medical revolution it enabled — above all smallpox vaccination, reaching ordinary life as state power through Britain’s compulsory Vaccination Acts — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. Toward vaccination he was a documented skeptic: treating it as “a purely statistical question,” he examined the mortality figures himself and condemned the practice and its penal enforcement, insisting official assurances “must never be accepted without verification.” The posture is double-edged, and that is what instructs: his statistical case was found erroneous by the Royal Commission and later epidemiology, vaccination among scientific medicine’s great successes — a reminder that data-literate, principled dissent can still reach the wrong conclusion.
figures.epoch: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913) was a British naturalist who, independently of Charles Darwin, arrived at the principle of natural selection, making him a co-discoverer of evolution by natural selection. Largely self-taught across surveying, natural history and statistics, he spent years collecting in the Amazon and the Malay Archipelago before returning to a public career in British science. His authority extended well beyond biology: in The Wonderful Century (1898) he surveyed and celebrated his era's scientific triumphs, and his autobiography My Life (1905) records a restless intellect drawn to heterodox causes. He was also a committed social reformer, serving as the first president of the Land Nationalisation Society (1881) and arguing, in Land Nationalisation (1882), that land was a common inheritance. By the 1890s he was a prominent public figure in British science.

title.en: AI data centres' electricity to double by 2030, more than all of Japan
title.fr: L'électricité des centres de données de l'IA doublera d'ici 2030, plus que la consommation de tout le Japon

text.en: The International Energy Agency's April 2025 report "Energy and AI" projects that global data-centre electricity demand will roughly double to about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030 — slightly more than Japan's entire electricity consumption today. This complicates the claim that AI will help solve climate change: the tool meant to help fight emissions is itself a fast-growing source of electricity demand. In the debate, this is the authoritative counterpoint — AI may aid some grand challenges while worsening the resource footprint of others.
text.fr: Le rapport « Energy and AI » de l'Agence internationale de l'énergie (avril 2025) prévoit que la demande mondiale d'électricité des centres de données doublera environ pour atteindre près de 945 térawattheures d'ici 2030 — un peu plus que la consommation électrique totale du Japon aujourd'hui. Cela complique l'idée que l'IA aidera à résoudre le changement climatique : l'outil censé aider à combattre les émissions est lui-même une source à croissance rapide de demande électrique. Dans le débat, c'est le contrepoint faisant autorité — l'IA peut aider certains grands défis tout en aggravant l'empreinte d'autres.

arguments.reference: IEA report "Energy and AI" and accompanying news release, 10 April 2025

Elle est le point d'identification du jeune spectateur cultivé scientifiquement qui se méfie du récit d'amélioration sans verser dans la panique.

title.en: Nuclear power's 1954 promises never came; why believe AI's ten-year promises?
title.fr: Les promesses nucléaires de 1954 ne sont jamais venues ; pourquoi croire celles de l'IA à dix ans ?

arguments.person: Lewis L. Strauss, Chairman of the US Atomic Energy Commission

text.en: In September 1954, Lewis Strauss, chairman of the US Atomic Energy Commission, told science writers that the atomic age would shortly deliver electricity too cheap to meter, famines known only as history, and much longer lifespans. Seventy years later, none of these everyday-life promises materialised on anything like that horizon. The historical pattern — revolutionary technologies systematically overpromising on the ten-to-twenty-year everyday horizon — is the strongest documented reason for discounting similar promises made today for AI.
text.fr: En septembre 1954, Lewis Strauss, président de la Commission américaine à l'énergie atomique, annonçait aux journalistes scientifiques que l'ère atomique apporterait bientôt une électricité trop bon marché pour être facturée, des famines reléguées aux livres d'histoire et des vies bien plus longues. Soixante-dix ans plus tard, aucune de ces promesses de vie quotidienne ne s'est réalisée à un tel horizon. Ce schéma historique — les technologies révolutionnaires surpromettent systématiquement à l'horizon de dix à vingt ans — est la raison documentée la plus forte pour relativiser les promesses analogues faites aujourd'hui pour l'IA.

arguments.reference: Speech to the National Association of Science Writers, New York, 16 September 1954; documented by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission
arguments.quote: It is not too much to expect that our children will enjoy in their homes electrical energy too cheap to meter, will know of great periodic regional famines in the world only as matters of history, will travel effortlessly over the seas and under them and through the air with a minimum of danger and at great speeds, and will experience a lifespan far longer than ours [...]

justification.en: For the first time a majority society expected a technology to do more harm than good. Hiroshima (1945), the Doomsday Clock (1947), the 'Duck and Cover' drills (1951), atmospheric tests and the Cuban crisis (1962) installed a lasting mass fear: 1950s polls gave a majority of Americans and Europeans judging a nuclear war likely in their lifetime. 'Atoms for Peace' (1953) did not reverse that horizon; the collective expectation was catastrophe, contained by treaties rather than dispelled.
justification.fr: Pour la première fois une société majoritaire s'attend à ce qu'une technologie fasse plus de mal que de bien. Hiroshima (1945), l'horloge de l'Apocalypse (1947), les exercices « Duck and Cover » (1951), les essais atmosphériques et la crise de Cuba (1962) installent une peur de masse durable : les sondages des années 1950 donnent une majorité d'Américains et d'Européens jugeant probable une guerre nucléaire de leur vivant. Le programme « Atoms for Peace » (1953) ne renverse pas cet horizon ; l'attente collective est la catastrophe, contenue par des traités plutôt que dissipée.

justification.en: First welcomed as the victory over hunger and insects (DDT, Nobel Prize 1948), synthetic chemistry turned in public opinion with Silent Spring (1962), thalidomide (1961) and the oil spills; the first Earth Day (1970, some 20 million participants in the United States) and then the DDT ban (1972) sealed a lasting majority reversal: the technosphere was now seen as a risk to contain, not as a promise.
justification.fr: Accueillie d'abord comme la victoire sur la faim et les insectes (DDT, prix Nobel 1948), la chimie de synthèse bascule dans l'opinion avec Silent Spring (1962), la thalidomide (1961) et les marées noires ; le premier Earth Day (1970, ~20 millions de participants aux États-Unis) puis l'interdiction du DDT (1972) sanctionnent un renversement majoritaire et durable : la technosphère est désormais perçue comme un risque à contenir, non comme une promesse.

figures.name: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti
figures.presentation: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti (1876–1944), Italian poet and impresario of the avant-garde, founded Futurism with the 1909 manifesto on the front page of Le Figaro. His wave was the motor-aviation complex — racing car, aeroplane, the whole machine age of speed — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was unqualified exaltation, the wave’s machine-worship extreme: “a roaring motor car… is more beautiful than the Victory of Samothrace,” “Time and Space died yesterday,” danger and rupture embraced as first principles. He instructs as a limit case: a genuine aesthetic response to a new technology hardening into a doctrine that scorns caution, restraint and every voice of the past. The disclosure is plain: Marinetti co-founded the Fasci italiani di combattimento in 1919 and co-authored the Fascist manifesto, and the 1909 text glorifies war and voices “contempt for woman” — documentary richness, never a moral example.
figures.epoch: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti (born Alexandria, Egypt, 22 December 1876; died Bellagio, 2 December 1944) was an Italian poet and cultural agitator who founded the Futurist movement with the manifesto he published on the front page of the Paris daily Le Figaro on 20 February 1909, after a first Italian printing in the Gazzetta dell'Emilia of Bologna earlier that month. Writing across French and Italian, he extended the movement's programme through his 1911 essay Multiplied Man and the Reign of the Machine (collected in Le Futurisme), the Technical Manifesto of Futurist Literature (1912), and the typographic sound-poem Zang Tumb Tuuum (1914), the last drawn from his own reporting on the 1912 Siege of Adrianople. His standing in the pre-war avant-garde rested less on a single masterwork than on his role as impresario and theorist of a self-declared break with the museums, academies and inherited culture of his day.

quote.en: We declare that the splendor of the world has been enriched by a new beauty: the beauty of speed. A racing automobile … a roaring motor car which seems to run on machine-gun fire, is more beautiful than the Victory of Samothrace.

figures.name: Henri de Saint-Simon
figures.presentation: Saint-Simon (1760–1825), French social reformer and publicist of post-Revolutionary France, argued from the Lettres d’un habitant de Genève (1802) to the Nouveau christianisme (1825) that society be led by its most capable producers. His wave was industrialisation — machine, factory and positive science reordering economic life — this study’s mirror for today’s AI: a technology that forces a society to decide who directs it and to what end. His stance was the enthusiast’s: the productive class “la fleur de la société,” direction to pass from an idle governing class to “les plus capables,” bound late to a moral precept — improving the lot of the poorest and most numerous class. Read forward, rule-by-capacity is plainly an ancestor of technocracy, a lineage neither endorsed nor laundered here — though he wrote in his own brakes, men “governed the least possible.” What instructs: greeting a general-purpose technology as an engine of shared betterment while entrusting its direction to demonstrated expertise — a bet the AI debate now revisits.
figures.epoch: Claude Henri de Rouvroy, comte de Saint-Simon (1760–1825), was a French social reformer and publicist active in the intellectual ferment of post-Revolutionary and Restoration France. He was a writer and doctrinaire rather than an engineer or laboratory scientist; his standing rested on a sequence of programmatic essays that circulated among savants and reform-minded readers. His first published work, the anonymous Lettres d'un habitant de Genève à ses contemporains (1802/1803), proposed that society entrust its leadership to its most capable men of science and art. Over the following two decades appeared the writings for which he is remembered: L'Organisateur (1819), containing the celebrated "parabole"; Du système industriel (1821); the Catéchisme des industriels (1823); and, in the year of his death, Nouveau christianisme (1825).

figures.name: Nikola Tesla
figures.presentation: Nikola Tesla (1856–1943), Serbian-American inventor, built the electrical age and then extrapolated it to planetary scale: power without wires, distance “virtually eliminated,” the earth imagined as “a huge brain.” For thirty-five years his documented stance held constant: human progress is the increase of human energy, and the machine is its means — applied to peace, agriculture and a coming technological millennium. That enthusiasm coexisted with a distrust of institutions, which he expected technology itself to render unnecessary. The dossier discloses the blind spots plainly — including eugenicist remarks in late interviews, in no way endorsed: his case shows both the generative power and the characteristic failures of unqualified technological optimism.
figures.epoch: Nikola Tesla (1856–1943), a Serbian-American inventor and electrical engineer, worked at the frontier of the electrical age in the United States. His standing rests less on institutional office than on a body of applied work and signed prose: the programmatic essay The Problem of Increasing Human Energy (Century Illustrated Magazine, June 1900), the peace essay The Transmission of Electrical Energy Without Wires (Electrical World and Engineer, 1905), and the autobiography My Inventions, serialized in Electrical Experimenter in 1919. His documentary anchor as a builder is U.S. Patent 613,809 (filed and granted 1898) for the radio-controlled boat — the telautomaton — publicly demonstrated at the 1898 Electrical Exhibition in Madison Square Garden. Across these sources he appears as a working inventor who both practised and prophesied the new art of applied electricity, and who addressed a wide public through the popular and trade press of his day.

title.en: Lasting AI damage is not inevitable: Europe already bans the worst uses by law
title.fr: Les dégâts durables de l'IA ne sont pas une fatalité : l'Europe interdit déjà les pires usages par la loi

arguments.person: European Parliament and Council of the European Union

text.en: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation 2024/1689), in force since August 2024, is the world's first comprehensive AI law. It grades systems from minimal to unacceptable risk, outright bans practices such as social scoring, and imposes strict duties on high-risk uses, with penalties up to 35 million euros or 7 percent of global turnover. Its existence is the counter-argument to the lasting-damage thesis: harmful uses are precisely those society is now legally structured to prevent, so durable damage is a policy failure to be avoided, not a foregone conclusion.
text.fr: Le règlement européen sur l'intelligence artificielle (Règlement 2024/1689), en vigueur depuis août 2024, est la première loi complète sur l'IA au monde. Il classe les systèmes du risque minimal au risque inacceptable, interdit purement des pratiques comme la notation sociale, et impose des obligations strictes aux usages à haut risque, avec des amendes allant jusqu'à 35 millions d'euros ou 7 % du chiffre d'affaires mondial. Son existence est le contre-argument à la thèse du dommage durable : les usages nuisibles sont précisément ceux que la société est désormais légalement organisée pour prévenir, si bien que le dommage durable est un échec de politique publique à éviter, non une fatalité.

arguments.reference: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of 13 June 2024, published in the Official Journal 12 July 2024; in force 1 August 2024

title.en: A YouTube channel with 8 million subscribers argues AI will make daily life better

Toute sa chaîne — plus de 8 millions d'abonnés — est conçue comme l'exact opposé de la dystopie technologique : rigoureusement documentée, mais convaincue que l'IA et d'autres technologies peuvent améliorer la vie quotidienne. Elle est le point d'identification du répondant qui vit ce débat sur YouTube, et non dans les revues savantes.

title.en: AI is as fundamental as the PC and Internet: daily life changes within years
title.fr: L'IA est aussi fondamentale que le PC et Internet : la vie quotidienne change en quelques années

arguments.person: Bill Gates, co-founder of Microsoft, philanthropist

text.en: In March 2023, Bill Gates wrote that in his whole life he had seen only two technology demonstrations that struck him as revolutionary: the graphical user interface in 1980, and OpenAI's GPT-4. Having driven the PC revolution himself, he predicts concrete effects on ordinary life within years, not centuries — work, learning, travel, health care, communication. His personal track record of correctly betting on the PC and the Internet is what gives this ten-year everyday-life forecast its weight in the debate.
text.fr: En mars 2023, Bill Gates écrivait que, de toute sa vie, seules deux démonstrations technologiques lui avaient semblé révolutionnaires : l'interface graphique en 1980, et GPT-4 d'OpenAI. Ayant lui-même conduit la révolution du PC, il prédit des effets concrets sur la vie ordinaire en quelques années, pas en quelques siècles — travail, apprentissage, voyages, santé, communication. Son bilan personnel — avoir parié juste sur le PC et Internet — donne son poids à cette prévision à dix ans sur la vie quotidienne.

arguments.reference: GatesNotes blog, essay "The Age of AI Has Begun", 21 March 2023
arguments.quote: The development of AI is as fundamental as the creation of the microprocessor, the personal computer, the Internet, and the mobile phone. It will change the way people work, learn, travel, get health care, and communicate with each other.

justification.en: No wave was welcomed with such unanimous and lasting collective faith. From the first power stations (Pearl Street, 1882) to the Chicago Exposition (1893) and the Palais de l'Électricité in Paris (1900), electricity was lived as the 'fairy' abolishing night, fatigue and coal grime: cities, industrialists, doctors and households demanded it rather than endured it. Accidents and the ruin of the lamplighters produced no lasting opposition; for thirty years, modernity was electrification.
justification.fr: Aucune vague n'a été accueillie avec une foi collective aussi unanime et aussi longue. Des premières centrales (Pearl Street, 1882) à l'Exposition de Chicago (1893) et au Palais de l'Électricité de Paris (1900), l'électricité est vécue comme la « fée » qui abolit la nuit, la fatigue et la crasse du charbon : villes, industriels, médecins et ménages la réclament plutôt qu'ils ne la subissent. Les accidents et la ruine des allumeurs de réverbères ne produisent aucun mouvement d'opposition durable ; trente ans durant, la modernité est l'électrification.

justification.en: From the 'information society' promised by governments (information superhighways, 1993–94) to the stock-market bubble (1995–2000) and Wikipedia (2001), majority opinion expected the network to bring more solutions than problems: free knowledge, participatory democracy, the end of intermediaries. Connected US households rose from about 18% (1997) to 55% (2003) without organised resistance; criticism (digital divide, surveillance, addiction) stayed marginal until the end of the period.
justification.fr: De la « société de l'information » promise par les gouvernements (autoroutes de l'information, 1993–94) à la bulle boursière (1995–2000) puis à Wikipédia (2001), l'opinion majoritaire attend du réseau plus de solutions que de problèmes — savoir gratuit, démocratie participative, fin des intermédiaires. Les foyers américains connectés passent d'environ 18 % (1997) à 55 % (2003) sans résistance organisée ; la critique (fracture numérique, surveillance, addiction) reste minoritaire jusqu'à la fin de la période.

synthesis.en: When I judge an AI system, my feelings and moral values matter more to me than the numbers.
synthesis.fr: Quand je juge un système d'IA, mon ressenti et mes valeurs morales comptent davantage pour moi que les chiffres.
synthesis.de: Wenn ich ein KI-System beurteile, zählen meine Gefühle und meine moralischen Werte für mich mehr als die Zahlen.

text.en: What I feel about an AI system matters more to me than the statistics about it.
text.fr: Ce que je ressens à propos d'un système d'IA compte davantage pour moi que les statistiques à son sujet.
text.de: Was ich bei einem KI-System empfinde, zählt für mich mehr als die Statistiken darüber.

clarification.en: This statement compares the weight you give to two things about an AI system: what you feel about it, and the statistics about it. It asks whether your feelings carry more weight than the statistics for you; it does not ask you to reject either one.
clarification.fr: Cet énoncé compare le poids que vous donnez à deux choses à propos d'un système d'IA : ce que vous ressentez à son sujet, et les statistiques à son sujet. Il demande si votre ressenti pèse davantage que les statistiques pour vous ; il ne demande pas d'écarter l'un ou l'autre.
clarification.de: Diese Aussage vergleicht das Gewicht, das Sie zwei Dingen bei einem KI-System geben: dem, was Sie dabei empfinden, und den Statistiken darüber. Sie fragt, ob Ihr Empfinden für Sie schwerer wiegt als die Statistiken; sie verlangt nicht, das eine oder das andere zu verwerfen.

anchor_low.en: Answering 0 means the statistics count clearly more for you than what you feel about an AI system.
anchor_low.fr: Répondre 0 signifie que les statistiques comptent nettement plus pour vous que ce que vous ressentez à propos d'un système d'IA.
anchor_low.de: Eine Antwort mit 0 bedeutet, dass die Statistiken für Sie deutlich mehr zählen als das, was Sie bei einem KI-System empfinden.

anchor_high.en: Answering 5 means what you feel about an AI system clearly counts more for you than the statistics about it.
anchor_high.fr: Répondre 5 signifie que ce que vous ressentez à propos d'un système d'IA compte nettement plus pour vous que les statistiques à son sujet.
anchor_high.de: Eine Antwort mit 5 bedeutet, dass das, was Sie bei einem KI-System empfinden, für Sie deutlich mehr zählt als die Statistiken darüber.

examples.en: For example, when an AI app gives health advice, does your sense of trust weigh more than its published accuracy figures, or do the figures weigh more?
examples.fr: Par exemple, quand une application d'IA donne des conseils de santé, votre sentiment de confiance pèse-t-il plus que ses chiffres de fiabilité publiés, ou les chiffres pèsent-ils plus ?
examples.de: Zum Beispiel: Wenn eine KI-App Gesundheitsratschläge gibt – wiegt Ihr Gefühl von Vertrauen schwerer als ihre veröffentlichten Genauigkeitswerte, oder wiegen die Zahlen schwerer?

examples.en: For example, is your view on AI cameras in public places shaped more by how being filmed makes you feel, or more by the published figures?
examples.fr: Par exemple, votre opinion sur les caméras à IA dans les lieux publics est-elle façonnée davantage par ce que le fait d'être filmé vous fait ressentir, ou davantage par les chiffres publiés ?
examples.de: Zum Beispiel: Wird Ihre Meinung über KI-Kameras an öffentlichen Orten stärker davon geprägt, wie es sich für Sie anfühlt, gefilmt zu werden, oder stärker von den veröffentlichten Zahlen?

text.en: Decisions about AI should above all respect moral values, even when the numbers point elsewhere.
text.fr: Les décisions sur l'IA devraient avant tout respecter des valeurs morales, même quand les chiffres indiquent autre chose.
text.de: Bei Entscheidungen über KI sollten vor allem moralische Werte geachtet werden, auch wenn die Zahlen in eine andere Richtung weisen.

clarification.en: This statement is about what should come first when moral values and measured results pull in different directions in a decision about AI. It is about that conflict situation, not about ordinary cases where values and numbers agree.
clarification.fr: Cet énoncé porte sur ce qui devrait passer en premier quand, dans une décision sur l'IA, les valeurs morales et les résultats mesurés tirent dans des directions différentes. Il concerne cette situation de conflit, pas les cas ordinaires où valeurs et chiffres vont dans le même sens.
clarification.de: Diese Aussage betrifft die Frage, was Vorrang haben sollte, wenn moralische Werte und gemessene Ergebnisse bei einer Entscheidung über KI in verschiedene Richtungen ziehen. Es geht um diese Konfliktsituation, nicht um die gewöhnlichen Fälle, in denen Werte und Zahlen übereinstimmen.

anchor_low.en: Answering 0 means you firmly think the measured results should prevail when they conflict with moral values.
anchor_low.fr: Répondre 0 signifie que vous pensez fermement que les résultats mesurés devraient l'emporter quand ils entrent en conflit avec des valeurs morales.
anchor_low.de: Eine Antwort mit 0 bedeutet, dass Sie fest der Meinung sind, die gemessenen Ergebnisse sollten den Ausschlag geben, wenn sie mit moralischen Werten in Konflikt geraten.

anchor_high.en: Answering 5 means you firmly think moral values should come first, even when the measured results point the other way.
anchor_high.fr: Répondre 5 signifie que vous pensez fermement que les valeurs morales devraient passer en premier, même quand les résultats mesurés indiquent l'inverse.
anchor_high.de: Eine Antwort mit 5 bedeutet, dass Sie fest der Meinung sind, moralische Werte sollten Vorrang haben, auch wenn die gemessenen Ergebnisse in die andere Richtung weisen.

examples.en: For example, declining an AI system that ranks people at work because it goes against one's values, even if the figures show it improves results — or accepting it because the figures are good.
examples.fr: Par exemple, refuser un système d'IA qui classe les personnes au travail parce qu'il va contre ses valeurs, même si les chiffres montrent qu'il améliore les résultats — ou l'accepter parce que les chiffres sont bons.
examples.de: Zum Beispiel ein KI-System ablehnen, das Menschen am Arbeitsplatz in eine Rangfolge bringt, weil es den eigenen Werten widerspricht, selbst wenn die Zahlen zeigen, dass es die Ergebnisse verbessert – oder es akzeptieren, weil die Zahlen gut sind.

examples.en: For example, accepting an AI that assigns intensive-care beds so as to maximise the number of lives saved because the outcome is measurably better — or refusing it because scoring patients goes against the principle that every life counts equally.
examples.fr: Par exemple, accepter une IA qui attribue les lits de soins intensifs de façon à maximiser le nombre de vies sauvées parce que le résultat est mesurablement meilleur — ou la refuser parce que noter des patients va contre le principe que chaque vie compte également.
examples.de: Zum Beispiel eine KI akzeptieren, die Intensivbetten so zuteilt, dass möglichst viele Leben gerettet werden, weil das Ergebnis messbar besser ist – oder sie ablehnen, weil das Bewerten von Erkrankten nach Punkten gegen den Grundsatz verstößt, dass jedes Leben gleich zählt.

text.en: When a technology makes me uneasy, I take that feeling seriously even without hard evidence.
text.fr: Quand une technologie me met mal à l'aise, je prends ce ressenti au sérieux même sans preuve tangible.
text.de: Wenn eine Technologie mir Unbehagen bereitet, nehme ich dieses Gefühl ernst, auch ohne handfeste Belege.

clarification.en: This statement is about how you treat your own unease about a technology when you have no hard evidence behind it: as a signal worth taking seriously, or as something to set aside until evidence appears. It does not say unease alone should decide everything.
clarification.fr: Cet énoncé porte sur la manière dont vous traitez votre propre malaise face à une technologie quand aucune preuve tangible ne l'appuie : comme un signal à prendre au sérieux, ou comme quelque chose à écarter tant qu'aucune preuve n'apparaît. Il ne dit pas que le malaise devrait tout décider à lui seul.
clarification.de: Diese Aussage betrifft den Umgang mit Ihrem eigenen Unbehagen gegenüber einer Technologie, wenn keine handfesten Belege dahinterstehen: als Signal, das es verdient, ernst genommen zu werden, oder als etwas, das man beiseiteschiebt, bis Belege auftauchen. Sie besagt nicht, dass Unbehagen allein alles entscheiden sollte.

anchor_low.en: Answering 0 means you firmly set your unease aside unless hard evidence supports it.
anchor_low.fr: Répondre 0 signifie que vous écartez fermement votre malaise tant qu'aucune preuve tangible ne l'appuie.
anchor_low.de: Eine Antwort mit 0 bedeutet, dass Sie Ihr Unbehagen konsequent beiseiteschieben, solange keine handfesten Belege es stützen.

anchor_high.en: Answering 5 means you firmly treat your unease as a serious signal, even when no hard evidence supports it.
anchor_high.fr: Répondre 5 signifie que vous traitez fermement votre malaise comme un signal sérieux, même quand aucune preuve tangible ne l'appuie.
anchor_high.de: Eine Antwort mit 5 bedeutet, dass Sie Ihr Unbehagen konsequent als ernstes Signal behandeln, auch wenn keine handfesten Belege es stützen.

examples.en: For example, feeling uneasy about an AI doll that talks with a child and acting on that feeling, or waiting for concrete signs of a problem before acting.
examples.fr: Par exemple, ressentir un malaise face à une poupée à IA qui parle avec un enfant et agir sur la base de ce ressenti, ou attendre des signes concrets de problème avant d'agir.
examples.de: Zum Beispiel Unbehagen gegenüber einer KI-Puppe empfinden, die mit einem Kind spricht, und aufgrund dieses Gefühls handeln – oder auf konkrete Anzeichen eines Problems warten, bevor Sie handeln.

examples.en: For example, feeling uneasy about an AI that records meetings and raising the issue on that basis alone, or raising it only once you can point to a proven problem.
examples.fr: Par exemple, ressentir un malaise face à une IA qui enregistre les réunions et soulever la question sur cette seule base, ou ne la soulever qu'une fois un problème avéré identifiable.

figures.name: Thomas Carlyle
figures.presentation: Thomas Carlyle (1795–1881), Scottish essayist and social critic, a prophetic public intellectual outside university and party, gave the age one of its lasting names: the “Mechanical Age.” His wave was industrialisation — the living artisan “driven from his workshop,” the “huge demon of Mechanism” oversetting multitudes of workmen, an England “full of wealth” yet “dying of inanition” — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was cultural and spiritual skepticism, not luddite refusal: he granted the material gains while diagnosing an inward loss, “men grown mechanical in head and in heart,” and asked for governance, not for turning back. Disclosure is owed: he also wrote the notorious racist pamphlet Occasional Discourse (1849/1853), excluded from the evidence corpus — selection for documentary richness, never as a moral model.
figures.epoch: Thomas Carlyle (1795-1881), born in Ecclefechan, Scotland, was an essayist, historian and social critic who became one of the most influential moral commentators of the early Victorian period. Writing first anonymously and then under his own name, he moved from the philosophical fiction of Sartor Resartus (serialised in Fraser's Magazine, 1833-34) to the social criticism of Chartism (1839) and Past and Present (1843), works through which, as later scholarship notes, he framed what came to be called the "Condition-of-England question" (Diniejko 2010). His 1829 Edinburgh Review essay "Signs of the Times" gave the age one of its enduring self-descriptions, the "Mechanical Age." Standing outside university and party, Carlyle exercised his authority as a prophetic public intellectual, and his diagnoses of industrial society shaped debate among his contemporaries well beyond literary circles.

figures.name: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
figures.presentation: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry (1900–1944), French aviator and writer, met the machine age from its frontier — night mail runs over the Sahara and South America, six thousand five hundred flying hours “under every sky in the world.” His stance is structurally two-sided: the aeroplane is “a tool, a tool like the plough,” an instrument of vision that “made us discover the true face of the earth” — while the machine-age civilisation around it threatened to reduce man to “robot-man, termite-man.” He welcomes the instrument and dreads the culture; the discipline he models is to separate the tool from the civilisation that deploys it, and to insist that man remain sovereign over both.
figures.epoch: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry (1900–1944) was a French aviator and writer whose literary standing grew directly out of his flying career. From 1926 he flew for the Compagnie Latécoère and its successor Aéropostale, serving as stopover chief at the Cap Juby desert outpost from 1927 and working the mail routes across the Sahara and South America. His books drew on that experience: Terre des hommes (1939), which received a prize from the Académie française, Pilote de guerre (1942, published in New York as Flight to Arras), Lettre à un otage (1943) and the fable Le Petit Prince (1943). By the early 1940s he was an established French writer whose books reached an international readership, several appearing first in New York. He returned to military reconnaissance in 1943–44 and disappeared on a mission on 31 July 1944. Two further works, Lettre au général X and Citadelle, appeared posthumously.

figures.name: Victor Hugo
figures.presentation: Victor Hugo (1802–1885), French poet, novelist and parliamentary voice — nineteen years an exile under the Second Empire — wrote as a poet-prophet whose judgements were moral and visionary. His wave was the coupling of railway, steamship and electric telegraph compressing Europe within a lifetime: he rode the new Antwerp–Brussels line in 1837, and by 1849 enrolled the same machines, “le fil électrique de la concorde,” in his vision of a federated, peaceful Europe. His stance was the ambivalent enthusiast’s: a providential faith in progress — “tomorrow cannot wait” — while the same 1837 letter that praised the train’s magnificent movement mourned “l’utile tout sec, jamais le beau.” What instructs is the pairing: embracing a transformative technology early while naming, in the same breath, a real cost to weigh against the gain — and measuring progress morally, by the elevation of the people, not efficiency alone.
figures.epoch: Victor Hugo (1802-1885) was a French poet, novelist and dramatist, and one of the defining voices of nineteenth-century French letters. His literary output spanned lyric verse, drama and the novel, and included the essay William Shakespeare (1864), a manifesto on genius and progress as much as a study of its title figure, and the Guernsey novel Les Travailleurs de la mer (1866). He was also a public and parliamentary figure: his speeches to the Assemblee legislative, later collected in Actes et paroles, argued for the destruction of destitution and for free, compulsory public schooling. His opposition to the Second Empire cost him nineteen years of exile (1851-1870). Across poetry, fiction and the political tribune, Hugo occupied a central place in the intellectual life of his era, writing as what the dossier calls a poet-prophet whose judgements were moral and visionary rather than measured.

text.en: Data scientist Cathy O'Neil, a former Wall Street quant, argues in Weapons of Math Destruction (2016) that the 'measurable facts' produced by algorithmic systems are not neutral: which data are collected, which proxies are chosen, and what counts as success all encode human value judgements. Her point challenges the idea that figures alone can ground an opinion of an AI system, since the figures themselves embed opinions.

Son argument conteste l'idée que les chiffres seuls puissent fonder une opinion sur un système d'IA, puisque les chiffres eux-mêmes incorporent des opinions.

figures.name: Edward Teller
figures.presentation: Edward Teller (1908–2003), Budapest-born American theoretical physicist, worked on the Manhattan Project, championed the hydrogen “Super” and helped found the Livermore weapons laboratory. His wave was the atom — weapons, reactors, fallout and test-ban debates — experienced as builder and adviser, this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was strong, consistent enthusiasm for development: cheap nuclear power “at any place on the globe,” the nuclear age answered by “understanding and courage,” not restraint or prohibition, which he judged unworkable — “nuclear secrets will not keep” — opposing the international control Einstein and Oppenheimer favoured. The disclosure is plain: he gave adverse testimony in the 1954 Oppenheimer security hearing and campaigned lifelong for the hydrogen bomb — a documented, controversial enthusiast pole, endorsed in neither respect. He instructs because his optimism was principled and articulate: a technologist’s conviction can illuminate a technology’s promise while carrying real costs that warrant scrutiny.
figures.epoch: Edward Teller (1908-2003), born in Budapest and later a naturalised American, was a theoretical physicist who worked on the wartime Manhattan Project and became widely identified as a principal architect of the hydrogen bomb. He served for decades inside the United States defence-science establishment, advising the Atomic Energy Commission and helping found and direct the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, a second weapons laboratory he pressed for against the existing Los Alamos monopoly. Beyond the classified programmes, he wrote for the public: 'Our Nuclear Future' (with Albert L. Latter, 1958), 'The Legacy of Hiroshima' (with Allen Brown, 1962), 'Better a Shield Than a Sword' (1987), and his 'Memoirs' (2001). He stood among the era's physicists as an outspoken, often isolated advocate of nuclear development, more comfortable arguing his case in policy and public forums than deferring to the scientific consensus that frequently opposed him.
