figures.name: Francis Bacon
figures.presentation: Francis Bacon (1561–1626), English lawyer, statesman and natural philosopher, rose to Lord Chancellor — until his 1621 conviction, confessed, for accepting gifts in judicial office — and wrote the programme of an organised, method-governed, state-supported experimental science, from The Advancement of Learning (1605) to the New Atlantis (1627). His wave was the “new science,” the turn from ancient authority to experiment, measured by printing, gunpowder and the compass, which had “changed the appearance and state of the whole world.” His enthusiasm was programmatic, not unconditional: knowledge for “the relief of man’s estate,” yet restrained — against rash anticipation and haste to profit, aware that innovations make losers as well as winners. What instructs is ambition coupled with method and moral governance.
figures.epoch: Francis Bacon (1561–1626) was an English lawyer, statesman and natural philosopher who rose through Elizabethan and Jacobean office to become Lord Chancellor; in 1621 he was impeached and convicted for accepting gifts while in judicial office, to which he confessed, and was removed from his post. His standing rests less on discoveries — he made none of the era's telescopic observations — than on a body of programmatic writing: The Advancement of Learning (1605), the Novum Organum issued within the unfinished Great Instauration (1620), the Essays or Counsels (1625), and the posthumously published New Atlantis (1627). Across these works he set out the case for an organised, method-governed, state-supported experimental science, addressing his plan directly to King James as its proper organiser.

figures.name: Fukuzawa Yukichi
figures.presentation: Fukuzawa Yukichi (1835–1901), Japanese writer and educator, founder of Keio-gijuku and among the most widely read voices of Meiji Japan, repeatedly declined office and remained a self-described commoner. His wave was industrialisation arriving as a shock — treaty ports, steam, telegraph, the whole of Western bunmei — this study’s mirror for today’s AI: a foreign, fast-arriving technology a society must decide how deeply to absorb. His stance was the enthusiast’s, yet ordered: adopting civilisation’s outward forms — schools, guns, machines — is useless unless a people first acquire its animating spirit; independence is the goal, techniques only the means. Disclosure is owed: he is also the probable author of the 1885 editorial Datsu-A Ron, read by later scholars as a charter of Japanese expansionism — selection for documentary richness, never as a moral model.
figures.epoch: Fukuzawa Yukichi (1835-1901) was a Japanese writer, educator and translator, and among the most widely read public intellectuals of Meiji Japan. Born into a lower-ranking samurai family, he trained first in Dutch learning at Ogata Koan's Osaka school, then — after finding Dutch useless before the English signs of newly opened Yokohama in 1859 — taught himself English, and travelled with early Japanese missions abroad, volunteering for the Kanrin Maru's 1860 Pacific crossing. In 1868 he founded the private academy Keio-gijuku (today Keio University) and in 1882 launched the newspaper Jiji Shimpo. His principal works — the seventeen pamphlets of An Encouragement of Learning (Gakumon no Susume, 1872-76), An Outline of a Theory of Civilization (Bunmeiron no Gairyaku, 1875), and his late Autobiography (1899) — reached a mass readership. He repeatedly declined government office, remaining a self-described commoner.

title.en: A physicist's 1883 maxim: judge AI by benchmarks and error rates, not impressions

text.en: In an 1883 lecture to the Institution of Civil Engineers, the physicist Lord Kelvin articulated the classic case for measurement as the foundation of knowledge. His maxim remains the canonical statement of the position that judgement of a technical system should rest on quantified facts. Applied to AI, it supports evaluating systems through benchmarks, error rates, and measured outcomes rather than impressions.
text.fr: Dans une conférence de 1883 devant l'Institution of Civil Engineers, le physicien Lord Kelvin a formulé l'argument classique faisant de la mesure le fondement de la connaissance. Sa maxime reste l'énoncé canonique de la position selon laquelle le jugement sur un système technique doit reposer sur des faits quantifiés. Appliquée à l'IA, elle soutient l'évaluation des systèmes par des bancs d'essai, des taux d'erreur et des résultats mesurés plutôt que par des impressions.

arguments.reference: Lecture 'Electrical Units of Measurement', Institution of Civil Engineers, 3 May 1883; in Popular Lectures and Addresses, vol. 1 (1889), pp. 80-81
arguments.quote: I often say that when you can measure what you are speaking about, and express it in numbers, you know something about it; but when you cannot measure it, when you cannot express it in numbers, your knowledge is of a meagre and unsatisfactory kind.

justification.en: The golden age of decision by calculation: operations research, cybernetics (Wiener, 1948), indicative planning, systems analysis (RAND), the Pentagon's 'whiz kids' (1961), programme budgeting (PPBS), the post-war boom managed 'by the numbers'. Governments, firms and much of public opinion then held measurement, cost and benefit to be the only legitimate basis of judgement, moral objections being dismissed as sentiment.
justification.fr: L'âge d'or de la décision par le calcul : recherche opérationnelle, cybernétique (Wiener, 1948), planification indicative, analyse de systèmes (RAND), whiz kids du Pentagone (1961), budgets programme (PPBS), Trente Glorieuses gérées « au chiffre ». Gouvernements, entreprises et une large part de l'opinion tiennent alors la mesure, le coût et le bénéfice pour l'unique base légitime du jugement, les objections morales étant renvoyées au sentiment.

justification.en: This is the wave that founded the criterion itself — reproducible observation against the authority of texts — and installed it durably in the academies (Nullius in verba, Royal Society, 1660) and then in learned opinion. The social majority followed only with delay (see Resistance), but the rational norm that emerged from it became irreversible.

La majorité sociale ne suit qu'avec retard (voir Résistance), mais la norme rationnelle qui en sort devient irréversible.

figures.name: Rachel Carson
figures.presentation: Rachel Carson (1907–1964), American marine biologist and science writer, confronted the postwar wave of synthetic pesticides — DDT and its kin, sprayed at scale with, as she wrote, little advance investigation of their effects on soil, water, wildlife and man. Silent Spring (1962) built its case on measured residue data and food-chain evidence, yet never demanded prohibition: “it is not my contention that chemical insecticides must never be used,” and her Senate testimony asked that aerial spraying be reduced to the minimum needed, not abolished. Her stance models calibrated precaution — rigorous evidence coupled with the citizen's right to know and informed public consent, without collapsing into a blanket ban.
figures.epoch: Rachel Carson (1907-1964) was an American marine biologist and science writer. Her 1951 study of the oceans, The Sea Around Us, brought her wide readership and the National Book Award for Nonfiction in 1952; in her acceptance remarks she set out the credo that "the materials of science are the materials of life itself" and that science is public knowledge, not the "priestlike" preserve of the laboratory. That standing -- established well before her best-known work -- led Scripps College to invite her to deliver its commencement address in June 1962. Later that year she published Silent Spring (Houghton Mifflin, 1962), a landmark of modern environmental writing; its reception was such that CBS Reports devoted a national broadcast to her work in April 1963, shortly before she testified before a United States Senate subcommittee.

figures.name: Platon
figures.presentation: Plato (c. 428–348 BCE), Greek philosopher, witnessed the disruptive technology of his world — writing itself, moving thought out of memory and oral performance into external marks. His verdict, in the Phaedrus myth of Theuth, is the oldest critique of a cognitive technology: letters breed forgetfulness and offer “the appearance of wisdom, not true wisdom” — and the inventor is not the fit judge of his own invention. Yet he conceded writing's uses as reminder and archive, and was himself a prolific master of the medium he distrusted, engineering the written dialogue to imitate living thought. His discipline remains the instructive part: separate a tool's advertised benefit from its real effects on the mind.
figures.epoch: Plato (c. 428–348 BCE) was a Greek philosopher active in Athens across the late fifth and fourth centuries BCE, and a central figure of classical Greek thought. He composed roughly thirty written dialogues — among them the Republic, the Laws, the Statesman, the Timaeus and the Phaedrus, together with the Epistles (Letter VII) consulted here — in most of which Socrates is the principal speaker. Beyond their content, these works represent a formal achievement in their own right: Plato engineered a new written genre designed to imitate the movement of living dialectic on the page, giving philosophical argument a durable textual form. His standing rests less on a single doctrine than on this sustained body of composition, which set out positions on knowledge, the soul, art and the governance of the city that later readers returned to repeatedly.

figures.name: Hannah Arendt
figures.presentation: Hannah Arendt (1906–1975), German-born political theorist exiled to the United States, analysed how modern societies think, judge and act in common, from The Human Condition (1958) to “Lying in Politics” (1971). Her wave was the mid-century convergence of automation and computing — satellites, factory-emptying automation, “giant computers” — this study’s mirror for today’s AI, read as a philosopher of the public world, not a technician. Her stance was precise philosophical skepticism, not technophobia: the problem-solvers “did not judge, they calculated”; the danger lies not in the machines but in ourselves, a society of thoughtless creatures at the mercy of every gadget. What instructs is her program: “to think what we are doing,” refusing calculation as a substitute for judgment.
figures.epoch: Hannah Arendt (1906–1975) was a German-born political theorist who, after fleeing Nazi Germany, settled in the United States and became one of the twentieth century's influential thinkers on political action, authority, and the public realm. Her standing rests on a coherent body of work: The Human Condition (University of Chicago Press, 1958), the essays gathered in Between Past and Future — among them "The Crisis in Culture" and "The Crisis in Education" (Viking Press, 1961) — and On Revolution (Viking Press, 1963). She also wrote the widely debated Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963), the essay "Karl Jaspers: Citizen of the World?" text.en: Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration, adopted by the UN Conference on Environment and Development, codifies the precautionary approach: 'Where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation.' Transposed to AI, it grounds the position that when potential harms are serious or irreversible, one does not wait for real-world trial results before acting — study and prevention come first.
text.fr: Le principe 15 de la Déclaration de Rio de 1992, adoptée par la Conférence des Nations unies sur l'environnement et le développement, codifie l'approche de précaution : « En cas de risque de dommages graves ou irréversibles, l'absence de certitude scientifique absolue ne doit pas servir de prétexte pour remettre à plus tard l'adoption de mesures effectives visant à prévenir la dégradation de l'environnement. » Transposé à l'IA, il fonde la position selon laquelle, quand les dommages potentiels sont graves ou irréversibles, on n'attend pas les résultats d'essais en conditions réelles avant d'agir — l'étude et la prévention passent d'abord.

Her warning — that speed and scale are outrunning any assessment of bias, cost and exclusion — anchors the 'disagree' side in peer-reviewed research rather than fear. As an Ethiopian-born scientist she also brings a Global-South perspective on who bears the downside of rushed deployment.

Son avertissement — la vitesse et l'échelle dépassent toute évaluation des biais, des coûts et des exclusions — ancre le camp du « contre » dans la recherche évaluée par les pairs plutôt que dans la peur. Scientifique née en Éthiopie, elle apporte aussi un regard du Sud global sur ceux qui subissent les effets d'un déploiement précipité.

figures.name: Bertolt Brecht
figures.presentation: Bertolt Brecht (1898–1956), German playwright and theorist of epic theatre, treated the stage as an instrument of critical reason “in the scientific age.” His wave was mass media — Weimar radio and cinema, cultural production in the hands of broadcasters and film capital — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. He was a conditional, reformist enthusiast: radio was “one-sided when it should be two” and had to pass “from distribution to communication,” letting the listener speak as well as hear — but only once its ownership was transformed, since “only the State can organize this.” What instructs: he locates a technology’s value not in the apparatus but in who owns and organises it. That enthusiasm was inseparable from his committed Marxism, a position of the figure to weigh rather than adopt.
figures.epoch: Bertolt Brecht (1898–1956) was a German playwright, poet, and theatre theorist whose work reshaped the dramaturgy of the Weimar Republic and the decades that followed. Formed in the theatrical and literary milieu of 1920s Germany, he became the theorist of what he called epic theatre, codified in his mature essay "A Short Organum for the Theatre" (written 1948, published 1949), in which he defined the alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt) meant to keep "the spectator's intellect free and highly mobile." His output included The Threepenny Opera, over whose film adaptation he later litigated, and he worked as writer and collaborator across theatre, radio, and cinema. Committed to a Marxist reading of art and society, Brecht treated the playhouse as an instrument for critical reason "in the scientific age" rather than for emotional catharsis.

figures.name: Thomas Edison
figures.presentation: Thomas Edison (1847–1931), American inventor who made invention itself an organised industrial enterprise, built the phonograph and a standardised central-station lighting system. His wave was electricity — lamps, motors and generating stations moving from laboratory demonstration to contested public utility — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was pragmatic enthusiasm: an invention was worth what it did and what it sold, machinery “the greatest of emancipators,” tempered by method — one per cent inspiration, several thousand things that won’t work. Disclosure is owed: in the war of currents his camp ran a denigration campaign against alternating current, including public electrocutions of animals, his own 1889 article serving that commercial interest. He instructs by holding enthusiasm, empirical discipline and self-interest together — documentary richness, not a moral model.
figures.epoch: Thomas Alva Edison (1847-1931) was an American inventor and inventor-entrepreneur who made invention itself into an organised industrial enterprise. He worked at the centre of the United States' electrical and machine age and, by the late 1870s, had introduced the phonograph, which he set out and championed in his own article 'The Phonograph and Its Future' in The North American Review (1878), written months after building the device. He went on to develop an electric-lighting system organised around standardised central-station generation, alongside motors and machinery. His authorized biography (Dyer and Martin, 1910) and later collections such as The Diary and Sundry Observations (posthumous, 1948) record a figure whose standing rested less on theory than on a prolific record of working, marketable inventions.

figures.name: Galilée
figures.presentation: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), Italian mathematician and natural philosopher, heard a rumour of a Dutch spyglass, rebuilt a better instrument within weeks, turned it on the sky — and went from observation to published book in about eight weeks. He then spent decades defending “sense experiences and necessary demonstrations” against consecrated authority, mocking the philosophers who refused to look through the telescope. His posture is early, active adoption: trust instrument-aided evidence over inherited authority, and iterate in the open. The record also keeps its costs — a thirteen-year self-embargo out of fear of ridicule, the frank pursuit of patronage, and the coerced abjuration of 1633, evidence of the control regime he lived under.
figures.epoch: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) was an Italian mathematician and natural philosopher of the late Renaissance. By his own account in Il Saggiatore (1623), he was reappointed and confirmed for life in his professorship of mathematics at the University of Padua at double his previous salary, and he subsequently entered the service of the Medici court of Tuscany. His principal works span a compressed public career: the observational booklet Sidereus Nuncius (1610), the doctrinal Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615), the polemical Il Saggiatore (1623), and the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632). His earlier correspondence with Johannes Kepler (1597, 1610) documents that his Copernican convictions predate his fame and place him in exchange with a leading astronomer of the age. He worked within a world whose epistemic authority rested with the university Aristotelians and the doctrinal organs of Counter-Reformation Rome.

text.en: Ng gives the most cited technical objection to the statement: 'prove it's safe' is proving a negative, and no engineer can guarantee a general technology will never be misused. He does not reject safety, he redirects it, arguing we should regulate concrete applications (underwriting, healthcare, self-driving) rather than gate the underlying models.

Il ne rejette pas la sécurité, il la réoriente : réguler les applications concrètes (assurance, santé, conduite autonome) plutôt que verrouiller les modèles sous-jacents.

arguments.reference: Written Statement of Andrew Ng before the US Senate AI Insight Forum (6 December 2023), republished by AI Fund. Primary source: schumer.senate.gov PDF.
arguments.quote: Trying to prove that it can't is akin to proving a negative. I am no more able to prove that AI won't kill us all than prove that radio waves emitted from our planet won't cause space aliens to find us and wipe us out.

title.en: Slowing AI delays cures, safety gains and prosperity: the techno-optimist manifesto
title.fr: Freiner l'IA retarde les remèdes, les gains de sûreté et la prospérité : le manifeste techno-optimiste

arguments.person: Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz

text.en: In 'The Techno-Optimist Manifesto' (a16z.com, October 2023), Marc Andreessen — co-creator of the first mass-market web browser and co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz — states the strongest public case for speed: delaying AI delays cures, safety improvements and prosperity that AI would otherwise deliver. The moderator should note this is the deliberately provocative pole of the accelerationist position, widely debated after publication.
text.fr: Dans « The Techno-Optimist Manifesto » (a16z.com, octobre 2023), Marc Andreessen — co-créateur du premier navigateur web grand public et cofondateur d'Andreessen Horowitz — formule le plaidoyer public le plus fort en faveur de la vitesse : retarder l'IA retarde les traitements, les gains de sécurité et la prospérité qu'elle apporterait. Le modérateur notera qu'il s'agit du pôle délibérément provocateur de la position accélérationniste, largement débattu après publication.

arguments.reference: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto, a16z.com, 16 October 2023
arguments.quote: We believe any deceleration of AI will cost lives. Deaths that were preventable by the AI that was prevented from existing is a form of murder.

justification.en: The 'railway mania' is the fastest and most unanimous engagement of societies in a revolution: in a single year (1846) the British Parliament authorised over 4,000 miles of line, the network tripled between 1843 and 1850, the United States passed 30,000 miles in 1860; the telegraph went from the Baltimore–Washington line (1844) to the transatlantic cable (1858, succeeding in 1866). All of it was deployed before the rules: signalling, brakes, company liability and standards came after the accidents, and the pace of adoption never slackened.
justification.fr: La « railway mania » est l'engagement le plus rapide et le plus unanime des sociétés dans une révolution : le Parlement britannique autorise en une seule année (1846) plus de 4 000 miles de lignes, le réseau triple entre 1843 et 1850, les États-Unis dépassent 30 000 miles en 1860 ; le télégraphe passe de la ligne Baltimore–Washington (1844) au câble transatlantique (1858, réussi en 1866). Tout cela se déploie avant les règles : signalisation, freins, responsabilité des compagnies et normalisation viennent après les accidents, sans que la vitesse d'adoption ne fléchisse.

justification.en: The motor car arrived before the driving licence (no driving test in the United Kingdom until 1935), before a unified highway code and before adapted roads; society improved the machine through use — brakes, tyres, lighting, the seat belt much later — accepting tens of thousands of deaths a year as the price of the first versions.
justification.fr: L'automobile arrive avant le permis (examen de conduite inexistant au Royaume-Uni jusqu'en 1935), avant le code de la route unifié et avant la voirie adaptée ; la société améliore la machine à l'usage — freins, pneus, éclairage, ceinture bien plus tard — en acceptant des dizaines de milliers de morts par an comme prix des premières versions.

figures.name: Neil Postman
figures.presentation: Neil Postman (1931–2003), American educator and cultural critic, built across Amusing Ourselves to Death (1985) and Technopoly (1992) a sustained critique of a culture reorganising itself around the screen. His wave was the personal computer and the networked information machine, promoted as a cure for information scarcity — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was cultural-critical skepticism, not luddism: “every technology is both a burden and a blessing,” each innovation “a Faustian bargain” carrying an embedded epistemological, political or social prejudice — proceed “with our eyes wide open so that we may use technology rather than be used by it.” He supplied the practical instrument — what is the problem to which this technology is the solution, and whose problem is it? — and lived the posture, writing longhand, owning no computer. What instructs is the discipline: name the trade-offs, ask who benefits, require a tool to justify itself before adoption.
figures.epoch: Neil Postman (1931–2003) was an American educator and cultural critic whose trade books made him one of his era's more widely read commentators on media and technology. Across the 1980s and 1990s he built a sustained critique of a culture reorganising itself around the screen and the machine. His best-known work, Amusing Ourselves to Death (Viking Penguin, 1985), examined a public discourse remade by television; Technopoly: The Surrender of Culture to Technology (Alfred A. Knopf, 1992) extended the argument to computing; and The End of Education (1995) and Building a Bridge to the 18th Century (1999) set out the cultural and educational ends against which he measured any new tool. His 1998 Denver address, "Five Things We Need to Know About Technological Change," distilled the theory into five compact propositions. He wrote as a public intellectual addressing parents, teachers and citizens rather than as a technical specialist.

figures.name: Henry David Thoreau
figures.presentation: Henry David Thoreau (1817–1862), American essayist and naturalist, lived beside his era's disruptive infrastructure — the railroad ran along Walden Pond during his stay, the telegraph hummed over his walks in Concord. His scepticism aimed at ends, seldom at capability: inventions as “improved means to an unimproved end,” the warning that “men have become the tools of their tools,” the priced refusal — “the swiftest traveller is he that goes afoot.” Yet the same pages record genuine wonder at the passing freight train and the wire's harp-like hum. He judges a technology by the human ends it advances and the attention it costs — never by adopting or rejecting it wholesale.
figures.epoch: Henry David Thoreau (1817-1862) was an American essayist, lecturer and naturalist writing from Concord, Massachusetts, in the orbit of New England Transcendentalism. His reputation rests on a compact body of prose: Walden; or, Life in the Woods (Ticknor and Fields, 1854), the account of his 1845-1847 stay in a self-built cabin beside Walden Pond; the essay "Resistance to Civil Government" (1849, later titled "Civil Disobedience"); the anti-slavery address "Slavery in Massachusetts" (1854); and the posthumously published lectures "Walking" (1862) and "Life Without Principle" (1863). His decades-long Journal, edited by Bradford Torrey (1906), records his daily observation. He also worked as a land surveyor, and the sounding survey of Walden Pond he describes shows a practiced facility with compass, chain and instrument. His standing grew chiefly after his death; in his lifetime he was a regional lecturer and writer rather than a widely celebrated figure.

figures.name: Georges Duhamel
figures.presentation: Georges Duhamel (1884–1966), French physician turned man of letters — war surgeon of 1914–1918, Prix Goncourt 1918, elected to the Académie française in 1935 — wrote from inside both establishments. His wave was the motor-and-machine civilisation of 1900–1940: assembly line, standardisation, cinema and radio, met head-on during his 1929 American journey — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was humanist-cultural skepticism: American cinema a “divertissement d’ilotes,” standardised culture “musique de conserve,” “la contagion de la machine” the coming world’s greatest peril. Yet no luddite: he mocked the despiser of progress, and as a doctor granted that mechanised medicine is “fort bien.” What instructs: a technically literate insider criticising the civilisation, not the tool.
figures.epoch: Georges Duhamel (1884-1966) was a French physician who became one of the established men of letters of the interwar Republic. Holding a doctorate in medicine, he served as a volunteer army surgeon in mobile surgical units (autochirs) throughout 1914-1918, an experience he turned into two celebrated books: Vie des martyrs (Mercure de France, 1917) and Civilisation, 1914-1917, which won the Prix Goncourt in 1918. He afterwards abandoned medicine for a full literary career, publishing novels, essays and travel accounts. His standing was institutionally consecrated when he was elected to the Academie francaise (fauteuil 30) on 21 November 1935, and he became a free member of the Academie de medecine from 1937. A doctor by training and a humanist by vocation, he wrote from within both the scientific and the literary establishments of his time.

text.en: Ortiz gives the 'disagree' pole a woman's voice from inside a creative profession. Offered a technology sold as faster and cheaper, she declines to change how she works and argues the craft itself is the point. Her stance is measured and argued — about consent and human voice — not mere technophobia, which is why it resonates with many working artists.

Devant une technologie vendue comme plus rapide et moins chère, elle refuse de changer sa manière de travailler et soutient que le métier lui-même est l'essentiel. Sa position est argumentée — consentement, voix humaine — et non une simple technophobie, ce qui explique son écho chez de nombreux artistes.

Elle offre aux répondants prudents une voix rigoureuse et sans hystérie.

title.en: 1811: skilled weavers broke machines that cut wages; a lesson for AI today

text.en: The Luddites (England, 1811-1816) were skilled textile workers — 'neither opposed to technology nor inept at using it' (Smithsonian Magazine) — who broke machines used, in their words as edited by Kevin Binfield, 'in a fraudulent and deceitful manner' to undercut wages and craft standards. Historian Eric Hobsbawm (1952) described their machine-breaking as 'collective bargaining by riot', not hostility to machines as such. Their case shows that defending proven ways of working can be a rational strategy against changes imposed on disadvantageous terms.
text.fr: Les luddites (Angleterre, 1811-1816) étaient des ouvriers textiles qualifiés — « ni opposés à la technologie, ni incapables de s'en servir » (Smithsonian Magazine) — qui brisaient les machines utilisées, selon leurs écrits édités par Kevin Binfield, « de manière frauduleuse et trompeuse » pour tirer vers le bas salaires et normes du métier. L'historien Eric Hobsbawm (1952) a décrit ce bris de machines comme une « négociation collective par l'émeute », et non une hostilité aux machines en soi. Leur cas montre que défendre des méthodes de travail éprouvées peut être une stratégie rationnelle face à des changements imposés à des conditions défavorables.

arguments.reference: Smithsonian Magazine, March 2011; E. J. Hobsbawm, 'The Machine Breakers', Past and Present 1(1), 1952, pp. 57-70

justification.en: The canonical example of a society keeping its proven ways: Bi Sheng invented movable type (c. 1040, as reported by Shen Kuo), yet for eight centuries Chinese workshops went on preferring woodblock printing, suited to thousands of characters and to abundant labour. The technology existed, was known and described, and society adopted it only when it had no other choice — under the pressure of Western typography in the 19th century.
justification.fr: L'exemple canonique de la société qui garde ses façons de faire éprouvées : Bi Sheng invente les caractères mobiles (v. 1040, rapporté par Shen Kuo), mais les ateliers chinois continuent pendant huit siècles à préférer la xylographie, adaptée à des milliers de sinogrammes et à une main-d'œuvre abondante. La technologie existe, elle est connue et décrite, et la société ne l'adopte que lorsqu'elle n'a plus d'autre choix — sous la pression de la typographie occidentale au XIXe siècle.

justification.en: The majority of the learned world (universities, teaching orders, the Congregation of the Index) refused for half a century to replace the Aristotelian corpus with instrumented observation — the decree of 1616, the trial of 1633, Descartes withholding Le Monde (1633). Openness was the work of a minority network of correspondents; the institution's dominant posture was holding on to the known.
justification.fr: Le monde savant majoritaire (universités, ordres enseignants, Congrégation de l'Index) refuse pendant un demi-siècle de substituer l'observation instrumentée au corpus aristotélicien — décret de 1616, procès de 1633, Descartes qui renonce à publier Le Monde (1633). L'ouverture est le fait d'un réseau de correspondants minoritaire ; la posture dominante de l'institution est le maintien du connu.

clarification.de: Diese Aussage betrifft das, was Sie tatsächlich gern tun: neue KI-Tools früh auszuprobieren, sobald sie für Sie verfügbar sind. Es geht um Ihre persönliche Freude am Ausprobieren, nicht darum, ob solche Tools Ihrer Ansicht nach gut oder schlecht für die Gesellschaft sind.

figures.name: Tim Berners-Lee
figures.presentation: Tim Berners-Lee (b. 1955), English computer scientist, invented the World Wide Web at CERN (1989–1991) and made the decision that shaped it: releasing its standards royalty-free, open for anyone to build on. The wave he set in motion turned a network of machines into a universal information space — then drifted, as he documented himself, toward data silos and a few dominant platforms. His answer is the disillusioned optimist's: naming the Web's dysfunctions in his anniversary letters, then building remedies — Solid, Inrupt, the Contract for the Web — to re-decentralise personal data. He models optimism as conditional and revisable: a hope held open to evidence, paired with the labour of repair.
figures.epoch: Tim Berners-Lee (b. 1955, England) is an English computer scientist who, while working at CERN between 1989 and 1991, designed and built the first Web browser and server together with the HTTP and HTML specifications that define the World Wide Web. In 1994 he founded the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), the standards body he continued to shape for decades, and in 1999 he set out the project's founding vision in the memoir Weaving the Web. The 2017 ACM A.M. Turing Award citation recognised the fundamental protocols and algorithms allowing the Web to scale. Across five decades he remained an active builder rather than a retired founder, launching the Solid project and the company Inrupt in 2018. His standing rests less on a single discovery than on a sustained decision, documented in his own account, to release the Web's standards royalty-free — kept open for anyone to implement without patent or fee.

figures.name: Norbert Wiener
figures.presentation: Norbert Wiener (1894–1964), American mathematician and founder of cybernetics, specified early computer design and helped build cybernetic prostheses — the technology arrived through his own hands. His wave was the high-speed computing machine and the automation it made possible, his “second industrial revolution,” spreading into factory, governance and warfare — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was cautionary rather than pessimistic: automation a “two-edged sword,” a learning machine able to outrun its designer, and once an irreversible process is launched “we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire.” He set moral “know-what” above technical “know-how,” and in 1947 refused to supply guided-missile research he judged dangerous. What instructs is technical fluency paired with restraint: those best placed to build a powerful technology may owe the clearest account of what it should not be trusted to decide.
figures.epoch: Norbert Wiener (1894–1964) was an American mathematician who founded the discipline of cybernetics — the study of control and communication in the animal and the machine — set out in his 1948 treatise of that name. Beyond pure mathematics, he helped design early computing machinery: a 1940 design memorandum to Vannevar Bush specified a numerical, electronic, base-two, fully automatic machine whose principles entered the modern computer, and, as he records in God & Golem, he later took part in the group work that developed cybernetic prostheses such as the myoelectric artificial hand. His principal works span the technical (Cybernetics, 1948) and the popular-philosophical (The Human Use of Human Beings, 1950; God & Golem, Inc., 1964, awarded the 1965 National Book Award posthumously). By mid-century he was both an originator of the new science and a widely read public interpreter of it.

figures.name: Louis Pasteur
figures.presentation: Louis Pasteur (1822–1895), French chemist, was not a commentator on his era's disruptive wave but its principal architect: germ theory, and the medicine it made possible. His optimism was total — the new science as “a law of peace, of work, of salvation” — but never naive: enthusiasm, he insisted, must keep “a severe control as its inseparable companion.” His method was proof-first and public: at Pouilly-le-Fort he signed the protocol in advance and let a controlled trial decide before witnesses; at the human frontier he treated the child Joseph Meister “not without grave and cruel misgivings.” What instructs is the pairing: confident enthusiasm disciplined by demonstrated proof and restraint.
figures.epoch: Louis Pasteur (1822-1895) was a French chemist whose work reached from crystallography and fermentation into medicine. From the inaugural address he delivered at Douai in December 1854, marking the installation of the science faculty at Lille, to the reception speech he gave at the Academie francaise on 27 April 1882, taking Littre's seat and answered by Ernest Renan, he moved at the centre of France's scientific establishment. His Sorbonne conference of 7 April 1864 argued against spontaneous generation; his 1881 report to the Academie des sciences recorded the public anthrax-vaccine trial at Pouilly-le-Fort; and in November 1888 the Institut Pasteur was inaugurated in Paris before President Sadi Carnot. He held standing across the era's academies of sciences, of medicine, and the Academie francaise, both as an experimenter and as a public figure.

title.en: ChatGPT reached 100 million users two months after launch, faster than any app
title.fr: ChatGPT a atteint 100 millions d'utilisateurs deux mois après son lancement, plus vite que toute autre application

text.en: According to a UBS study reported by Reuters, ChatGPT reached an estimated 100 million monthly active users in January 2023, just two months after launch — the fastest-growing consumer application in history (TikTok needed about nine months, Instagram about two and a half years). Millions of ordinary people tried a brand-new AI tool the moment they could access it, showing that immediate experimentation is a widespread, not marginal, behaviour.
text.fr: Selon une étude UBS rapportée par Reuters, ChatGPT a atteint environ 100 millions d'utilisateurs actifs mensuels en janvier 2023, deux mois seulement après son lancement — l'application grand public à la croissance la plus rapide de l'histoire (TikTok avait mis environ neuf mois, Instagram environ deux ans et demi). Des millions de personnes ordinaires ont essayé un tout nouvel outil d'IA dès qu'elles y ont eu accès : l'expérimentation immédiate est un comportement répandu, non marginal.

arguments.reference: Reuters (Krystal Hu), 2 February 2023, citing UBS/Similarweb

title.en: We will be newbies forever: grab each new AI tool as it appears
title.fr: Nous serons débutants pour toujours : saisir chaque nouvel outil d'IA dès qu'il paraît

arguments.person: Kevin Kelly, founding executive editor of Wired

text.en: Kevin Kelly, founding executive editor of Wired, argues in The Inevitable (2016) that because technology is now in permanent flux, everyone is condemned to be a beginner again and again. Rather than a burden, he presents this endless cycle of trying, upgrading and re-learning as the normal and desirable condition of contemporary life — the disposition of someone who reaches for each new tool as it appears.
text.fr: Kevin Kelly, rédacteur en chef fondateur de Wired, soutient dans The Inevitable (2016) que, la technologie étant désormais en flux permanent, chacun est condamné à redevenir débutant encore et encore. Loin d'un fardeau, il présente ce cycle sans fin d'essais, de mises à jour et de réapprentissages comme la condition normale et désirable de la vie contemporaine — la disposition de celui qui saisit chaque nouvel outil dès son apparition.

arguments.reference: The Inevitable, ch. 1 'Becoming', Viking, 2016
arguments.quote: In this era of becoming, everyone becomes a newbie. Worse, we will be newbies forever.

title.en: Tested the newest AI model, Claude 5 Fable, the moment it was released

text.en: Mollick remains the scholarly face of earliest-possible adoption: handed access to a just-released model, he stress-tested it across real projects rather than waiting for others' verdicts. For a respondent who rushes to every new tool, his 2026 hands-on write-up is the up-to-date intellectual justification.
text.fr: Mollick reste le visage universitaire de l'adoption la plus précoce possible : ayant obtenu l'accès à un tout nouveau modèle, il l'a immédiatement mis à l'épreuve sur des projets réels plutôt que d'attendre les avis d'autrui. Pour un répondant qui se rue sur chaque nouvel outil, son compte rendu pratique de 2026 offre la justification intellectuelle la plus actuelle.

justification.en: Adoption was massive, enthusiastic and unconstrained: 15 million Ford Model Ts (1908–1927), one vehicle for every five Americans in 1929, millions of drivers learning an unknown machine on their own before any driving school existed. Aviation was celebrated as popular spectacle — Blériot (1909), Lindbergh welcomed by four million New Yorkers (1927) — and mechanics became a mass hobby (clubs, races, garages). Society did not wait to have 'no other choice': it tried.
justification.fr: L'adoption est massive, enthousiaste et sans contrainte : 15 millions de Ford T (1908–1927), un véhicule pour cinq Américains en 1929, des millions de conducteurs apprenant seuls une machine inconnue avant toute école de conduite. L'aviation est fêtée comme un spectacle populaire — Blériot (1909), Lindbergh accueilli par quatre millions de New-Yorkais (1927) — et la mécanique devient un loisir de masse (clubs, courses, garages). La société n'attend pas d'avoir « le choix » : elle essaie.

justification.en: Radio went from almost zero (1921) to over 40% of American households (1930) and 80% (1940), in the middle of the Depression; the talkies (1927) replaced silent film in three years and the weekly cinema became the ritual of tens of millions of Europeans. A wholly new technology was tamed at home, out of curiosity, without economic necessity.
justification.fr: La radio passe de quasi zéro (1921) à plus de 40 % des foyers américains (1930) et 80 % (1940), en pleine Dépression ; le cinéma parlant (1927) remplace le muet en trois ans et le cinéma hebdomadaire devient le rite de dizaines de millions d'Européens. Une technologie totalement nouvelle est apprivoisée chez soi, par curiosité, sans nécessité économique.

text.en: Everyone should remain free to use AI as they see fit.

clarification.en: This statement is about each person deciding for themselves how to use AI, without others setting limits. It asks whether that personal freedom should be the general rule; it does not say what people would actually do with it.
clarification.fr: Cet énoncé porte sur le fait que chaque personne décide elle-même de son usage de l'IA, sans que d'autres fixent des limites. Il demande si cette liberté personnelle devrait être la règle générale ; il ne dit pas ce que les gens en feraient réellement.
clarification.de: Diese Aussage betrifft den Umstand, dass jede Person selbst entscheidet, wie sie KI nutzt, ohne dass andere Grenzen setzen. Sie fragt, ob diese persönliche Freiheit die allgemeine Regel sein sollte; sie sagt nicht, was die Menschen damit tatsächlich tun würden.

anchor_low.en: Answering 0 means you firmly reject the idea that everyone can use AI as they wish; for you, clear limits set by others are needed.
anchor_low.fr: Répondre 0 signifie que vous rejetez fermement l'idée que chacun puisse utiliser l'IA comme il le souhaite ; pour vous, des limites claires fixées par d'autres sont nécessaires.

anchor_high.en: Answering 5 means you fully support letting each person use AI as they see fit, without outside limits on their choices.
anchor_high.fr: Répondre 5 signifie que vous soutenez pleinement que chaque personne utilise l'IA comme elle l'entend, sans limites extérieures sur ses choix.
anchor_high.de: Mit 5 zu antworten bedeutet, dass Sie voll und ganz unterstützen, dass jede Person KI so nutzt, wie sie es für richtig hält, ohne äußere Grenzen für ihre Entscheidungen.

figures.name: George Orwell
figures.presentation: George Orwell (1903–1950), English essayist and novelist, watched the mass-media wave — radio and cinema reaching millions at once — from the inside as a BBC producer, and against it as its most lucid critic. What alarmed him was never the apparatus but its concentration: expensive, few-controlled media that make the strong stronger and centralise power over opinion. His posture is accept-but-distrust: the machine had to be accepted “as one accepts a drug — grudgingly and suspiciously”; he used radio to bring poetry to a wide audience while scrutinising who controlled it, and later dramatised its surveillance potential in Nineteen Eighty-Four. Work with the tool, concede its usefulness — and never stop questioning the power gathered around it.
figures.epoch: George Orwell (1903-1950), the English essayist and novelist born Eric Blair, worked chiefly as a journalist and writer of documentary prose. His standing rested on a body of reportage, essays and fiction: the 1937 documentary and polemic The Road to Wigan Pier, whose second part is a sustained first-person reckoning with machine civilisation, and the 1949 dystopia Nineteen Eighty-Four are the principal works this study draws on. Between 1941 and 1943 he served as a Talks Producer at the BBC, producing literary programmes broadcast to India, and through the mid-1940s he published a stream of essays in Tribune, Polemic, Horizon and The New Saxon Pamphlet. Writing at once from inside the era's information institutions and against their concentration, he occupied the position of a working practitioner-critic of mass communication rather than a detached observer.

figures.name: Walt Whitman
figures.presentation: Walt Whitman (1819–1892), American poet of Leaves of Grass, took the industrial, democratic republic itself as his subject. His wave was the coupling of railroad and telegraph — the transcontinental line and Suez Canal of 1869, the Atlantic cable — “the distant brought near,” this study’s mirror for today’s AI. His stance was enthusiastic, and spiritual before material: in “Passage to India” these works fulfil “God’s purpose from the first,” valued “not for trade or transportation only”; the locomotive hailed as “Type of the modern.” Yet Democratic Vistas called the materially triumphant Union “canker’d, crude, superstitious, and rotten” wherever the moral and spiritual layer was missing — a documented counterweight kept in view. What instructs is the condition attached to the enthusiasm: embracing a transformative technology wholeheartedly while insisting that material triumph is not, by itself, sufficient.
figures.epoch: Walt Whitman (1819-1892) was an American poet whose collection Leaves of Grass, first issued in 1855 and enlarged across successive editions through the 1891-92 "deathbed" edition, made him a central voice of nineteenth-century American letters. The 1855 volume opened with the poem left untitled there and later called "Song of Myself." His work spanned verse and prose: the 1871 pamphlet Democratic Vistas set out his reflections on American democracy, and he wrote for public occasions, reciting the poem later titled "Song of the Exposition" at the opening of the 40th Annual Exhibition of the American Institute in New York on 7 September 1871. Across the 1860s and 1870s his poems increasingly took the industrial, democratic republic itself as their subject, making him, on the documentary record, a poet closely engaged with the machinery of his age rather than turned away from it.

figures.name: Yann LeCun
figures.presentation: Yann LeCun (born 1960), French-American computer scientist, built early convolutional networks in 1989, shared the 2018 Turing Award, served as Meta’s Chief AI Scientist until 2025, then founded AMI Labs. His wave is artificial intelligence itself — the deep-learning renaissance he helped construct, mirror and subject coinciding. His stance is the builder-optimist’s, separating enthusiasm from governance: “there is no evidence” of existential risk, he told the UN Security Council in 2024; regulate products, not research; defend open source against corporate concentration — and even set aside the dominant large-language-model paradigm as an “off-ramp” to human-level AI. What instructs is the method: evidence over alarm, and readiness to revise a reigning paradigm. A living figure whose positions still shift; his open-source advocacy through 2025 was voiced from a leadership post at the company whose models he defended — an interest overlap disclosed here.
figures.epoch: Yann LeCun, born in 1960 in France and later based in the United States, is a computer scientist who became one of the central architects of modern machine learning. He built early convolutional neural networks in 1989, an approach that would underpin the deep-learning methods adopted across the field from 2012 onward, and he received the 2018 Turing Award for this line of work. From 2013 to 2025 he served as Chief AI Scientist at Meta, one of the most visible research-leadership positions in the industry, while remaining a professor at New York University. In 2022 he issued the position paper "A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence," arguing for world-model and joint-embedding architectures rather than the reigning paradigm. In November 2025 he left Meta to found AMI Labs, unveiled in 2026 with a large seed round, continuing that research programme independently.

text.en: Donelan is a cabinet-level policymaker who chose the opposite path to the EU: no rush to strict statutory AI rules. Pressed by MPs in December 2023, she insisted that legislating too fast would stifle innovation and that the technology must first be properly understood. She lets a respondent see that opposing strict rules is a mainstream governing position, defended in Parliament, not merely an industry talking point.
text.fr: Donelan est une responsable politique de premier plan qui a choisi la voie inverse de celle de l'UE : pas de précipitation vers des règles légales strictes sur l'IA. Interrogée par des députés en décembre 2023, elle a soutenu que légiférer trop vite étoufferait l'innovation et qu'il fallait d'abord bien comprendre la technologie. Elle montre à un répondant que s'opposer à des règles strictes est une position de gouvernement courante, défendue au Parlement, et pas seulement un argument de l'industrie.

arguments.person: Yann LeCun, Chief AI Scientist at Meta, Turing Award laureate

text.en: Ahead of the November 2023 Bletchley Park summit, Turing Award laureate Yann LeCun, then Meta's chief AI scientist, publicly argued in a Financial Times interview that regulating AI research and development is counterproductive: premature restrictions rest on unproven danger scenarios, would entrench the dominance of a few large companies, and would stifle the open-source competition that keeps AI accountable. His documented position is the leading scientific voice against prohibition-first approaches.
text.fr: À la veille du sommet de Bletchley Park de novembre 2023, le lauréat du prix Turing Yann LeCun, alors directeur scientifique de l'IA chez Meta, a publiquement soutenu dans un entretien au Financial Times que réguler la recherche et le développement en IA est contre-productif : des restrictions prématurées reposent sur des scénarios de danger non prouvés, consolideraient la domination de quelques grandes entreprises et étoufferaient la concurrence open source qui rend l'IA redevable. Sa position documentée est la principale voix scientifique contre les approches privilégiant l'interdiction.

arguments.reference: Interview with John Thornhill, Financial Times, 19 October 2023 (wording varies across reports; position paraphrased)

title.en: AI can prevent deaths, so any rule that slows it costs lives

arguments.person: Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz

text.en: In his 2023 'Techno-Optimist Manifesto', venture capitalist Marc Andreessen states the strongest form of the anti-restriction position: because AI can prevent deaths (in medicine, safety, poverty), rules that slow it down have a human cost of their own. The manifesto reframes the liberty/safety trade-off by arguing that restriction, not deployment, is what endangers people.
text.fr: Dans son « Manifeste techno-optimiste » de 2023, l'investisseur Marc Andreessen énonce la forme la plus forte de la position anti-restriction : parce que l'IA peut éviter des morts (médecine, sécurité, pauvreté), les règles qui la ralentissent ont elles-mêmes un coût humain. Le manifeste renverse l'arbitrage liberté/sécurité en soutenant que c'est la restriction, et non le déploiement, qui met les gens en danger.

arguments.reference: 'The Techno-Optimist Manifesto', a16z.com, October 2023

justification.en: Too much regulation then worried far more than too little: the Communications Decency Act was struck down (1997) to applause, hosting immunity (Section 230, 1996) commanded consensus, attempts at content control were denounced as censorship, and most users and industrialists claimed a right to use the network 'as they saw fit'. This libertarian posture remained dominant until the 2010s.
justification.fr: L'excès de régulation inquiète alors bien plus que son absence : le Communications Decency Act est invalidé (1997) sous les applaudissements, l'immunité des hébergeurs (Section 230, 1996) fait consensus, les tentatives de contrôle des contenus sont dénoncées comme censure, et la majorité des usagers comme des industriels revendique un droit d'utiliser le réseau « comme il l'entend ». Cette posture libertaire reste dominante jusqu'aux années 2010.

justification.en: The repeal of the Red Flag Act (1896, celebrated by the London–Brighton Emancipation Run), resistance to speed limits, freedom of the road raised to a value: society chose to let everyone use the machine at will and accepted regulation (licence, highway code, insurance) only by drips.

clarification.en: This statement is about rules on how AI is used, made by governments or other authorities, that everyone must follow. It asks whether you find such rules necessary even when they stop people from doing some things they would like to do; it is not about any specific law, nor about who should set the rules.
clarification.fr: Cet énoncé porte sur des règles d'usage de l'IA, fixées par les gouvernements ou d'autres autorités, que chacun doit respecter. Il demande si vous trouvez ces règles nécessaires même quand elles empêchent des personnes de faire certaines choses qu'elles voudraient faire ; il ne vise aucune loi en particulier, ni la question de savoir qui devrait fixer ces règles.
clarification.de: Diese Aussage betrifft Regeln für die Nutzung von KI, die von Regierungen oder anderen Instanzen festgelegt werden und die alle befolgen müssen. Sie fragt, ob Sie solche Regeln auch dann für notwendig halten, wenn sie Menschen daran hindern, manches zu tun, was sie gerne tun würden; es geht weder um ein bestimmtes Gesetz noch darum, wer die Regeln festlegen sollte.

figures.name: Karl Marx
figures.presentation: Karl Marx (1818–1883), German political economist and revolutionary organiser, analysed industrialisation not as an inventor but as a scholar — reading the factory inspectors' reports in London to trace how steam-driven machinery restructured labour. His stance is dialectical: the same machine is emancipatory in itself, gifted with “the wonderful power of shortening and fructifying human labour,” yet degrading in the hands of capital, where it lengthened the working day. He rejected the Luddite response — target the mode in which machines are used, never the instruments themselves — and backed factory legislation as society's conscious reaction. His enduring lesson: separate a technology's potential from the social arrangements that govern its deployment.
figures.epoch: Karl Marx (1818-1883), born in Germany, was a political economist, philosopher, and revolutionary organiser who devoted his mature working life to analysing the emerging industrial-capitalist order. With Friedrich Engels he issued the Manifesto of the Communist Party (1848); his principal work, Capital: A Critique of Political Economy, Volume I, appeared in 1867. He also drafted the founding texts of the International Working Men's Association -- its Inaugural Address (1864) and the Instructions for the delegates of the Geneva Congress (1866) -- writing these in English. His method rested on close reading of official statistics, parliamentary Blue Books, and the reports of the English factory inspectorate, which he re-argued through his own analysis. By the 1860s he stood among the more systematic critical theorists of industrial society, though his wider influence grew mostly after his death.

figures.name: Timnit Gebru
figures.presentation: Timnit Gebru (born 1983), computer scientist trained in Fei-Fei Li’s Stanford laboratory, co-led Google’s Ethical AI team, co-founded Black in AI and founded the DAIR institute — a builder of the technology turned insider-critic of the industry that produces it. Her wave is artificial intelligence itself, from the deep-learning turn to the large-language-model “gold rush” of ChatGPT, observed from within Apple, Microsoft and Google, then audited from outside. Her stance is critical-egalitarian, aimed at power and accountability rather than the technology in the abstract: AI’s harms are real, present and preventable; both existential-risk “fearmongering” and utopian AGI narratives are rejected; the demands are public oversight, transparency and attention to who bears the risks. A living figure still in motion, her account of her 2020 departure from Google remains disputed between the parties and is not adjudicated here.
figures.epoch: Timnit Gebru (born 1983 in Addis Ababa; Ethiopia/USA) is a computer scientist who became a prominent voice in the fairness-and-accountability wing of artificial-intelligence research. Trained as an engineer and an audio-hardware engineer at Apple, she earned a PhD in computer vision at Stanford in Fei-Fei Li's laboratory, then worked at Microsoft Research's FATE group before co-leading Google's Ethical AI team until December 2020. In 2017 she co-founded Black in AI, and in 2021 she founded the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR). Her principal works include the co-authored audit Gender Shades (2018), which measured accuracy disparities in commercial gender-classification systems; the influential FAccT paper On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots (2021); and, with Émile Torres, the 2024 essay naming the TESCREAL bundle (First Monday). She occupies the position of an insider-critic: a builder of the technology who turned to scrutinising the industry that produces it.

figures.name: Albert Einstein
figures.presentation: Albert Einstein (1879–1955), German-born theoretical physicist and later an American public conscience, signed the 1939 letter warning Roosevelt that uranium could yield extremely powerful bombs — then spent the decade after Hiroshima advocating supranational control of the very technology he had helped set in motion. He held both poles honestly: urging acceleration under fear of a German bomb, later calling that signature “one great mistake,” fearing the tyranny of world government yet fearing war more. His posture instructs less by its answers than by its demand: a technology of civilizational reach requires governance of matching scale, deliberated publicly rather than left to experts alone.
figures.epoch: Einstein (1879–1955), German-born and later American, was a theoretical physicist whose standing gave his signature alone the weight to reach a head of state: in August 1939 his letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, drafted with Leo Szilard, warned that uranium might become a new source of energy and yield extremely powerful bombs. He described himself not as "the father of the release of atomic energy" — his part, he said, was "quite indirect" — but as one who had judged that release was "theoretically possible." Beyond physics he was a public moral voice: chairman of the Emergency Committee of Atomic Scientists (1946), author of the social-philosophy essay "Why Socialism?" (Monthly Review, 1949), and, days before his death, co-signatory with Bertrand Russell of the 1955 manifesto calling on humanity to renounce war — the appeal from which the Pugwash Conferences arose, whose organisation preserves the text cited here. By the atomic decade his authority was as much civic as scientific.

text.en: At the first global AI Safety Summit (Bletchley Park, 1-2 November 2023), 28 countries and the EU — including both the United States and China — agreed that frontier AI systems should be subject to safety testing and evaluation, with governments playing a central oversight role. It is concrete evidence that monitoring of AI systems is broadly accepted internationally as a condition of collective safety, across rival political systems.

text.en: On 14 May 2019, San Francisco — the symbolic capital of the tech industry — became the first major US city to ban the use of facial recognition by its government agencies and police, judging the technology's risks to civil liberties to outweigh its claimed benefits. The 'Stop Secret Surveillance' ordinance shows a democratic community choosing outright prohibition of an AI application rather than mere discouragement, and it triggered similar bans in other US cities.
text.fr: Le 14 mai 2019, San Francisco — capitale symbolique de l'industrie technologique — est devenue la première grande ville américaine à interdire l'usage de la reconnaissance faciale par ses agences municipales et sa police, jugeant que les risques de cette technologie pour les libertés civiles l'emportaient sur ses bénéfices allégués. L'ordonnance « Stop Secret Surveillance » montre une communauté démocratique choisissant l'interdiction pure et simple d'une application de l'IA plutôt que sa simple dissuasion, et elle a déclenché des interdictions similaires dans d'autres villes américaines.

text.en: On 16 May 2023, OpenAI's own chief executive told the US Senate Judiciary Subcommittee that government-imposed rules on AI are not an obstacle but a necessity, proposing licensing and testing requirements for powerful models. Que le créateur de ChatGPT demande publiquement des contraintes contraignantes est un argument frappant en faveur de règles strictes, même au prix d'une certaine liberté d'action.

figures.name: Audrey Tang
figures.presentation: Audrey Tang (born 1981), Taiwanese programmer risen from the free-software world to become Taiwan’s first Digital Minister (2016–2024) and first openly non-binary cabinet member, distilled the island’s digital-democracy practice into Plurality (2024). Her wave is artificial intelligence itself, met from an unusual vantage — the engineer who builds the systems and the official who governs their public use, deploying AI-assisted “broad listening” for national-scale consultation while confronting deepfakes and algorithmic amplification. Her stance is democratic optimism conditional on democratic design: AI governance “must be a race to safety, not a race to power,” each community able to set its own norms, harms like “addictive intelligence” read as design choices that can be made otherwise. A living figure still in motion, she shows how a builder can advocate diffusion and precaution at once — catastrophe neither inevitable nor negligible, but contingent on institutions.
figures.epoch: Audrey Tang (born 1981 in Taipei) is a Taiwanese programmer and public servant who rose from the free-software world into government. A self-taught coder, she became a Silicon Valley software founder at nineteen and led the Pugs open-source project before entering Taiwan's civic-technology movement. In 2016 she was appointed Taiwan's first Digital Minister, a post she held until 2024, and she was the island's first openly non-binary cabinet member. Her fullest intellectual statement is the open-source book Plurality: The Future of Collaborative Technology and Democracy (2024), co-authored with the economist E. Glen Weyl and a wider contributor community, which distils Taiwan's digital-democracy practice — vTaiwan, the Polis opinion-clustering tool, the g0v civic-hacker movement — into a general design programme. She is best understood as a practitioner-theorist of participatory governance rather than an academic.

figures.name: José Martí
figures.presentation: José Martí (1853–1895), Cuban poet and journalist exiled in New York from 1880, chronicled the Gilded-Age metropolis for Latin American readers until his death in the Cuban war of independence he had helped organise. His wave was electricity and its engineering — Edison’s light, the telegraph, the Brooklyn Bridge he chronicled in 1883 — watched from inside the technological metropolis, yet as a Latin American outsider. His stance was genuinely double: delight at the new force — Edison a “Dantesque figure,” the Bridge “a ponderous arm of the human mind,” electricity soon to relieve suffering labour — while the same texts warn of a prosperity “empty of spirit” and insist his republics graft the world onto their own trunk rather than be absorbed. What instructs is the discipline: he knew that world “from inside” (viví en el monstruo), quantified it honestly, and refused both uncritical adoption and reflexive rejection.
figures.epoch: José Martí (1853-1895) was a Cuban poet, essayist and journalist. His principal texts of this period include the prologue to Pérez Bonalde's Poema del Niágara (1882), "Coney Island" (1881), "El puente de Brooklyn" (1883), the essay "Nuestra América" (1891) and "La verdad sobre los Estados Unidos" (1894); his last, unfinished letter to Manuel Mercado was written at Dos Ríos on 18 May 1895, the eve of his death in the Cuban war of independence he had helped organise. He remains a national figure of Cuba.

figures.name: Wangari Maathai
figures.presentation: Wangari Maathai (1940–2011), Kenyan biologist — the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate — founded the Green Belt Movement and received the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize. Her wave, read through her own testimony, was industrial, commercialised, top-down development: forests cleared for commercial plantations, household food crops displaced, public land grabbed — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. Her stance was precautionary, aimed at destructive, imposed development rather than technology as such: “there can be no development without sustainable management of the environment,” justice and ecological integrity worth more “than profits at any cost,” and agency located in the community — “solutions to most of our problems must come from us.” What instructs is less opposition to a technology than the insistence that its deployment be equitable, sustainable and locally governed; her Nobel lecture closed on conditional hope: “The choice is ours.”
figures.epoch: Wangari Maathai (1940-2011) was a Kenyan biologist and environmental campaigner. Trained as a research scientist, she was, per the dossier, the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate, later serving as a professor of veterinary anatomy. She founded the Green Belt Movement, a grassroots tree-planting and citizen-education initiative. As that year's laureate, she delivered the Nobel Peace Prize Lecture in Oslo on 10 December 2004. Her principal written works, the memoir Unbowed (2006), The Challenge for Africa (2009), and Replenishing the Earth (2010), set out her account of the movement, her critique of top-down development, and her spiritual environmentalism. She combined scientific credentials with sustained public activism, standing against the Kenyan state in campaigns such as the Uhuru Park (1989) and Karura Forest (1998-99) disputes.

arguments.person: Friedrich A. Hayek, economist, Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences 1974

text.en: In his classic 1945 essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society', economist and later Nobel laureate Friedrich Hayek argued that the knowledge relevant to economic and social decisions never exists in one place, but is scattered among countless individuals. This argument is regularly invoked against uniform top-down rule-making for fast-moving technologies: an international rule-setter would lack the local, contextual knowledge that dispersed decision-makers hold.
text.fr: Dans son essai classique de 1945, « The Use of Knowledge in Society », l'économiste et futur lauréat du prix Nobel Friedrich Hayek soutenait que le savoir pertinent pour les décisions économiques et sociales n'existe jamais en un seul lieu, mais est dispersé entre d'innombrables individus. Cet argument est régulièrement invoqué contre l'édiction de règles uniformes venues d'en haut pour des technologies en évolution rapide : un régulateur international manquerait du savoir local et contextuel détenu par des décideurs dispersés.

arguments.reference: American Economic Review, vol. 35, no. 4, September 1945, pp. 519–530 (full text verified at Econlib)
arguments.quote: The peculiar character of the problem of a rational economic order is determined precisely by the fact that the knowledge of the circumstances of which we must make use never exists in concentrated or integrated form but solely as the dispersed bits of incomplete and frequently contradictory knowledge which all the separate individuals possess.

figures.name: J. Robert Oppenheimer
figures.presentation: Robert Oppenheimer (1904–1967), American theoretical physicist, directed the Los Alamos laboratory where the first atomic weapons were built, then moved into postwar science policy — the Acheson-Lilienthal report, the AEC’s General Advisory Committee. His wave was the atom, reaching the world through his own hands and entering public consciousness with Hiroshima and Nagasaki — this study’s mirror for today’s AI as a dual-use capability contested first by its own makers. His stance was genuinely ambivalent: the work an “organic necessity,” yet within weeks of Hiroshima the warning that mankind would come to curse the names of Los Alamos and Hiroshima; in 1948, that the physicists had “known sin”; in 1949, the recommendation against the hydrogen Super, and candour and international control against secrecy. What instructs is measured, not heroic: a maker holding capability and restraint together, judging a technology while implicated in it.
figures.epoch: Julius Robert Oppenheimer (1904-1967) was an American theoretical physicist who became, during the Second World War, the scientific director of the Los Alamos laboratory, the centre where the first atomic weapons were designed and built. His standing rested less on a single discovery than on his ability to lead a large scientific community at the frontier of physics, and afterwards to speak for it in public life. From this base he moved into the institutions of postwar science policy: he was the principal scientific author of the 1946 Acheson-Lilienthal report on international control of atomic energy, and he chaired the General Advisory Committee of the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission. In 1953 he delivered the BBC Reith Lectures, published as Science and the Common Understanding. He was thus at once an insider who built the technology and a widely heard interpreter of what it meant.

figures.name: Ibn Khaldun
figures.wave: Crafts and techniques of urban civilisation
figures.presentation: Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406), Arab scholar, jurist and chief judge in Cairo, founded in the Muqaddima (1377) a new science of civilization explaining why societies rise, flourish and decay. The disruptive capability of his world was the crafts of settled urban life — building, writing, calculation, medicine — which he showed arise with the city and multiply where societies are large, stable and strongly governed. His stance is analytic rather than advocative: technique is a distinctively human power whose crafts “give intelligence” to their practitioners, yet whose perfection is tied to the life-cycle of civilization — they recede as the city declines. Neither boosterism nor alarm: a causal account of technology as inseparable from the social order that sustains it.
figures.epoch: Abd ar-Rahman Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406) was an Arab scholar, jurist and administrator born in Tunis, active across the Maghrib and later in Mamluk Egypt, where he served as a Maliki chief judge in Cairo. His standing rests on the Muqaddima (1377), the introductory volume of his universal history Kitab al-'Ibar, in which he set out to found a new science of human social organization ('umran) explaining why civilizations rise, flourish and decay. The publisher's description of Rosenthal's translation credits the work with having established the foundations of several fields, including the philosophy of history, sociology, ethnography and economics (Rosenthal 1958). Rather than a chronicler of dynasties, he presented himself as an analyst of their underlying causes, cross-checking transmitted reports against what a settled society could plausibly support.

figures.name: Érasme
figures.presentation: Erasmus (1466–1536), among the foremost humanists of the northern Renaissance, edited the first published Greek New Testament (1516) and lived inside Europe’s leading presses — Aldus in Venice, Froben in Basel — arguably the first author to build a career entirely on print. His wave was the printing press, multiplying texts at unprecedented speed and filling the world, as he complained, with “swarms of new books” of every quality — this study’s mirror for today’s AI. He was a critical adopter: among the technology’s heaviest professional users and one of its sharpest critics — printers “so grasping and mercenary” that errors stand — calling for public remedy: magistrates against abuse, law against fraud, subsidy for works of common use. One asymmetry is disclosed: he used the press fully for himself while at times seeking to limit others’ use of it.
figures.epoch: Desiderius Erasmus (1466-1536), born in the Netherlands, ranks among the foremost humanist scholars of the northern Renaissance. He built his career on classical and biblical philology, producing the Adagia (a continually expanded compendium of proverbs, from 1500), the Colloquies, and, in 1516, the Novum Instrumentum omne — the first published Greek New Testament, edited from the manuscript evidence rather than accepted on the authority of the received Vulgate (Froben, Basel). He worked inside the leading presses of Europe, living in Aldus Manutius's Venetian shop in 1508 and in Johann Froben's Basel household across 1514-1516 and again 1521-1529. His writings circulated on an unusual scale for the period — roughly 1,260 printings and reprintings before his death, on one scholarly estimate — making him arguably the first European author to build an entire career on the medium of print.
